speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret to again have to call the attention 'of the House, and especially the attention of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), to the fact that I am receiving complaints every day from farmers in various parts of the Dominion regarding the income tax return form, to the effect that although they are very anxious to make their returns, they cannot procure the forms in French. speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed -from April 22 consideration in committee of Bill No. 12-Hon. Mr. Guthrie-respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this Bill was
last before the committee, clause 22 and the proposed amendment of Mr. Fielding thereto were under discussion. Shall the amendment carry?

Mr. Chairman, I do not
want to protract unnecessarily the discussion of this clause, but I think that arguments have been advanced which should command the attention of the Government. Returning officers will have the power to nominate between two and. three hundred officials in each constituency-deputy returning officers, registrars, clerks, and so on. Is it fair that the Government should keep this patronage for themselves and their own nominees? We on this side are ready to receive any suggestion that may be made by the Government to make this clause more satisfactory. But if they insit upon the clause as it stands, I am afraid that we shall have to continue the debate as long as we can.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?
Lost.

If the minister thinks he
can make headway by not answering my suggestion, he is mistaken. If I have to stand here alone and object to the Bill, I will do it; I can do it until six o'clock if necessary. I repeat that we are ready to accept any suggestion which will provide for an independent nomination of the returning officer, who will have the nomination of between two and three hundred election officials in his constituency at each election. The hon. member (Mr. Fielding) has brought in an amendment. We do not contend it is the only remedy for the situation, but in my opinion something should he done.
. Mr. GUTHRIE: I thought that this subject was pretty fully discussed yesterday afternoon, and with all due respect to my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) I do not think he

has brought any new light to bear on it. One point that was made yesterday afternoon-or attempted to be made; it did not appeal to me-was that the Government should show some good ground for rejecting the proposal. My idea was that good ground should be shown why the old and tried system should not be retained. We have had a long experience under that system and I have yet to hear of more than one case of wrong-doing on the part of a returning officer. The only case that was brought to the attention of the committee was the case of West Elgin, in which the returning officer, the sheriff, was removed from his office for wrong-doing. It has been stated that wrong has undoubtedly been done in the past; yet only that one case has beerr cited. I think we may fairly take it for granted that the system has worked well in the past and that good ground should be shown for any change.

What about the patronage in the appointment of two or three hundred election officials in each constituency?
. Mr. GUTHRIE:	If you wish to call it
patronage, why do so. But I submit that returning officers who have been appointed 'in the past either by Liberal Governments or by Conservative Governments have fulfilled their duty under the Election. Act, whatever it involved, and ' I assume they will do it again. The Government must assume the responsibility for the conduct of an election. It would be hard for a government to carry that responsibility and yet have nothing to say as to the men who are to carry out the details ot the Act. There is only one way of doing it: the Government must advise His Excellency, who will appoint the returning officers. We ask nothing new; we do not seek to change the law in any way. This system has been tried and proved and has done well. If my hon. friend can show me that generally it has failed-I do not mean in isolated cases -then there may be something to be said in favour of the amendment, but the concensus of opinion yesterday was that the old system had worked well.

If my hon. friend wants a reason why the system should be changed, the one that strikes me most forcibly is that patronage has been abolished. This is the biggest plum in the patronage pie-the appointment of over 230 returning officers and of 100 enumerators by each of these, a total of 23,000 enumerators. There was nothing so large as that in the old patronage system. As I have said, patronage has been abolished; I myself heard the
Prime Minister abolish it two years ago, and on that occasion he was loudly cheered by hon. gentlemen on the other side. Now, this is a return to the old patronage system; it is diametrically opposed to the policy that the minister has been supporting. The ideal system would be to allow the general returning officer to select his own officials in each county to conduct the election; that would be placing the business entirely outside of politics. Apparently my hon. friend is not willing to do that. The amendment proposed to restrict the old patronage system to some extent, and I would expect the minister to accept that principle, because it is in line with the policy which he professes to follow. If we allow the Bill to go through as it is, it simply means that the Government are selecting a jury to try themselves. If the Government select as returning officers partisans in each of the counties and these partisans select one hundred more persons in each county to make the lists, that is equivalent, at any rate in cities and in close constituencies, to winning the election. That gives an immense advantage to the party in power, whatever party that may be; and if my hon. friend is desirous of avoiding criticism of that kind and is willing to give us a fair Bill, I can see no reason why he should not accept the proposal of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding).

In the past, prior to 1896, I remember well that we had, in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, returning officers who, to my mind, were not men who should have been entrusted with that responsible duty. They did one part of their work satisfactorily, but as regards the duty of paying out salaries to the deputy returning officers and their clerks, they were somewhat slow; and I know that on many occasions the deputy returning officers and their clerks were not paid their salaries, nor did the owners of the polling booths receive the rent to which they were entitled. During the period that I was sheriff, I had the honour of being appointed returning officer on different occasions, and my experience of elections is that I have had this complaint made to me so many times that to-day I ask The Government to appoint in each constituency as returning officer the most responsible man they can find, I do not care whether he be Conservative or Liberal, in order that all the deputy returning officers and their clerks may be sure of receiving their salaries and that the owners of the polling booths may be satisfied that they

will obtain their rent. When I took charge as returning officer, the people in many places where I was not well known throughout the county were not quite satisfied to rent their houses for the day on account of the rents of polling booths not having been paid in the past, and the consequence was that I had difficulty in securing places for polling booths in my county. The Provincial Government subdivides each county into polling divisions, and in each division they state that the. polling booth must be at or near a certain place which they name, and the polling booth cannot be placed in a different part of the polling division. That being the case, we have certain limited sections within which to select these polling booths. Moreover, on account of the way in which the lists are made up according to these divisions and as, the women being allowed to vote, there is a large addition to the electoral lists, the returning officer will have in each division three or four or even five polling booths in order to poll all the votes. Therefore, a man of responsibility should be appointed, so that he will carry on his duties in a satisfactory manner. I know that in many districts in the constituency which I represent, deputy returning officers overdid their duty by initialling the ballots outside, and these ballots were distributed and went from one to another when the voters were in the ante-room to mark their ballots. If the Government want to retain the patronage system and name one of their friends, I have no objection to that because each party has done that in the past; or if they want to do away with patronage as they say they do, although I am doubtful, what I have stated is a reason why, at any rate, they should appoint a responsible man.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
With the general trend of the remarks of my hon. friend, I quite agree, and I think I can assure him that the Government will see that in each case a responsible man in the community will be appointed. As regards the non-payment of fees to the minor election officials, the Bill recognizes that the system which was in force in the past was not a good system, and by clause 76, a new provision is made. Subclause 5 of clause 76 provides that after the fees have been adjusted,
Such fees, allowances and disbursements shall he paid by warrant of the Governor General and shall he distributed by such person or persons as the Governor General in Council may direct to the several officers and persons entitled thereto.
Payment in future will be made directly from Ottawa to the individual. Formerly, 
it went to the returning officers, and I have heard of cases where poll clerks, constables and those who had allowed their premises to be used as polling booths had great difficulty in obtaining payment. It is considered that this new clause will remedy that to a large extent.

I support the amendment moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) because of the experience I have had in my province as regards the contesting of elections. I do not know whether the same rule applies in other provinces, but in practically all cases in New Brunswick the returning officer is the high sheriff of the county. There have been exceptions to this rule, and I am bound to say that in New. Brunswick, so far as my experience goes, we had no trouble, even if somebody outside was selected by either Government which happened to have the responsibility of appointing returning officers. Good men have generally been selected, and I have no fault to find whatever as regards the men who have been selected. But my reason for referring particularly to the high sheriff as being the proper official to appoint as returning officer is the result of my experience of election contests in New Brunswick. I am speaking entirely in regard to my province, because I do not know what occurs in other provinces in that regard. In the election of 1917, the Government who were responsible for conducting that election in New Brunswick appointed the high sheriff in each county as returning officer. I may frankly say that the majority of these returning officers w'ere Liberals; some were Conservatives. In my constituency the returning officer wras a Liberal. He went through the county and after meeting local committees representing both sides he appointed the enumerators on their recommendation, as nearly as possible on a 50-50 basis. Throughout the whole province, where the returning officer was a Conservative he would have for his deputy a Liberal, and vice versa, and so on down the line. Both parties in this way were fairly represented at every poll. I think every representative from the province of New Brunswick in this House, irrespective of the party he supports, will agree with me that on the last election there was not one single case of wrong-doing or even of attempted wrongdoing throughout the province. I quite agree that it would not be well to confine these appointments to one particular class of official, because it might happen that the high sheriff of a particular county was

not the proper man for returning officer, but in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred he would he a very proper person to hold the poll and conduct the election fairly and honestly. In our province the-y have had the experience. They hold the ballot boxes from one -election to another and know the routine and the whole procedure of conducting an election. To my mind they are very proper persons to act as returning officers. The amendment covers a very much wider field, but I would not for a moment suggest that these other officials would not make proper returning officers, for they hold responsible positions in the community and would realize that the people looked to them to conduct the election in a straightforward and honest manner. I think the amendment proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) is a reasonable one, and I am sure he would have no objection to including other classes of officials in his amendment if the minister should so desire. The Government have announced that they want to abolish patronage, so I think they should be more than willing to accept any reasonable 'suggestion looking to the conducting of elections in a fair and honest manner, and without any suspicion of wrong-doing. When the Government and the Opposition and the third party go before the country, the people want the conduct of the election to be divorced from any possibility or suspicion of wrong-doing. I am sure my hon friend realizes that. They do not want somebody appointed returning officer or registrar who will do the wrong thing, appoint their own friends, for instance. We must take human nature as we find it. A returning officer who is a strong partisan, when the candidate in whose success he is interested asks him to appoint so-and-so as registrar in a certain polling division, would not be likely to refuse to appoint the man recommended, and if that registrar puts on the lists names that should not be there, or strikes others off that should be there, it is evident that we cannot have a fair test of the public mind.
Does the hon. member suggest that the candidate can recommend to the returning officer those whom be would like to have appointed as officials for the taking of the poll?
I was speaking of registrars.
In the case of a large constituency, .how would the returning officer know who would be proper persons to appoint as enumerators, poll clerks, and so on, at the different divisions?
How would my hon. friend suggest that he would find out?
The way it has been done in the past is for the candidate to tell the returning officer who are the people that should be appointed in the different localities.
That is exactly the point I was making. It is by that method that irregularities creep in. My hon. friend gives the whole case away.
How would the returning officer himself know whom to appoint?

He would go and see for himself. In our province the high sheriff has had long experience in conducting elections, and knows the men in the different localities whom he can trust to discharge faithfully and impartially the duties of the different offices. That is the very, reason why I am supporting this amendment. My hon. friend is perhaps speaking from experience. Perhaps that is what happened to my hon. friend in the last election.
It did.

That means that the Union Government candidates in the next election will have the say in making appointments, and not the returning officer. The candidates will have the selection of the registrars who will make up the voters' lists, and it is only human nature to expect them to appoint friends of their own party. That is one of the very best reasons we could have for supporting this amendment, so that the conduct of the election shall be taken out of the hands of the candidates themselves.

This is the first time, I think, that it has ever been contended in this House that the responsibility for the appointment of such an important officer should be abolished, for that is what the amendment means.

No.
Mr. CROTBER.S: Let us see. Suppose we pass a statute making it compulsory upon this Government to appoint a certain official, one .of those mentioned in the proposed amendment a sheriff, for instance. The sheriff goes wrong in the conduct of the election. Who is responsible? This

Government? No. This Government did not appoint him sheriff. He was appointed sheriff by the Government of British Columbia or some other province, and this Government would very properly say: We are not responsible for that fraudulent election; the sheriff was responsible; he took part in the fraud; we did not make him sheriff, and under an Act of this Parliament we were obliged to appoint him to the office he held. Now it must be obvious to every hon. gen-. tleman on the opposite side that if this amendment were adopted we should abolish entirely the responsibility that rests on this Government in the appointment of these officers. _What responsibility would the Government have if they appointed a man of their own choice who was not a sheriff and who proved incapable? They would be responsible both to this House and to the country for having appointed an inefficient man. But under my hon. friend's proposition they would be free from responsibility because they would be in a position to say-
They never admit responsibility anyway.
If this proposal were adopted you think the wrong man would be elected.

There is no logic in
that.
There is too much logic all around for you to answer.

I was about to say that it would be no answer to this Government's repudiation of responsibility to say that a man was appointed sheriff by the Government of Quebec or the Government of Ontario, or any other Government. This Government would be in a position to say: We are not responsible because we appointed an officer whom we were compelled to appoint under a statute passed by this House. My hon. friend (Mr. Copp) and the hon. member (Mr. Sinclair), said in substance that hon. members on this side of the House have expressed themselves as being in favour of the absolute abolition of patronage. That is not so. Patronage has not been absolutely abolished, and neither my hon. friends on the other side of the House-
Now, that is something new.
-nor hon. gentlemen on this side, have contended, so far as I know, that patronage should be absolutely abolished.
Our contention is that'you claim patronage to have been abolished, whereas in fact it has not.

You never contended that it ought to be abolished. I do not think that any hon. gentleman on the other side has ever suggested that the Government should not appoint a judge, one of the most important officers in the country. Have hon. gentlemen opposite ever contended that the Government should not appoint judges or senators by Order in Council? So that my hon. friends will see that patronage has not been abolished in toto, and there has never been any suggestion from either side o'f the House that it should be. This Government has exercised the power of appointing returning officers for fifty years. The Dominion Government, Liberal or Conservative as the case might be, has been responsible in the matter, and on the whole the system has worked perfectly satisfactorily. As my hon. friend, the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) has said, there has been only one case in the history of Canada where a man appointed returning officer for a constituency did not rise to the occasion and act honestly and with integrity between the two political parties, and that was in the case of West Elgin, the constituency which I have the honour to represent. That returning oflicer was appointed sheriff by the Liberal Government of Ontario, and he took an active part in defrauding the electors of that constituency of their choice of candidate to represent them in the legislature of the province of Ontario, and for that fraudulent conduct he was dismissed. So far as I know, from my own experience, that is the only instance in our history in which a returning officer failed to discharge his duties faithfully and well. Do we propose now, after the lapse of fifty years, to abolish a system that has worked exceedingly well? By whatever government, Liberal or Conservative, men have been appointed, there has been no question except, in that one case, of the intelligence and integrity of the appointee. What do my hon. friends say in substance? They say that the Dominion Government at Ottawa, either Liberal or Conservative, cannot be trusted to select a man to act as returning officer in any particular constituency, but we can implicitly trust a man named by the province of British Columbia, say. It is all right to appoint a sheriff nominated by the Government of Manitoba; it is all right to appoint a registrar of deeds appointed

by the Government of Nova Scotia or the Government of New Brunswick; but it is absolutely wrong for this Government to appoint any man. Any Provincial Government, no matter whether it be Liberal or Conservative, can safely be trusted to appoint a sheriff, a registrar of deed, a collector of customs, or a postmaster. They will all do; they are all intelligent; they are all honest. And there were three or four hon. gentlemen on the other side who took this view yesterday. The hon. member who moved the amendment said he knew a Conservative in Nova Scotia who had held a public office for forty-three years and who was a man of great intelligence and absolute integrity; and having served the public for forty-three years he was still a Conservative and an intelligent and honest man.
There may be some question about his intelligence.

And the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) also spoke of a man whom he knew in Sherbrooke, another Conservative who was absolutely honest and of whose integrity there could be no question. Now, how absurd it is for our hon. friends to say that we cannot trust a man appointed by the Government of Canada, although for fifty years the Dominion Government has appointed men who have proved perfectly capable and whose characters have been absolutely irreproachable. It will never do, we are told, to have the Government at Ottawa appoint men, because no confidence could be placed in them; but we must appoint men who have been appointed by the Provincial Government. If we adopted the amendment we would absolutely abolish the safeguard which the people of Canada have in the responsibility that this Government owes to them. A sheriff may be guilty of incalculable fraud, a man may be elected under him who should never have been elected, and who is not the choice of the people. But the answer comes from this Government: We are not responsible; the Government of Nova Scotia, for instance, appointed him sheriff and under the statute of this House we made him returning officer Every one will see the absurdity of the position which we are asked to take.

My hon. friend has talked about the responsibility of the Government. Well, this responsibility is purely mythical, as my hon. friend knows. Let us see what it really would amount to in practice. Suppose this amendment were 101
adopted and, in an election, a sheriff were appointed in any province in Canada as returning officer. Then let us suppose that our friends opposite were returned to power

we may do violence to our imagination to that extent for the sake of argument-and the hon. member, having come back to Parliament, finds that there is a charge that the sheriff had not conducted the election fairly and that there was reasonable ground fqr complaint agaiifst him. Somebody in this Parliament gets up and makes that charge. What answer would my hon. friend make? We would not have to stretch our imaginations very far to think of my hon friend getting up and saying: "We are responsible for it; that man was recommended to us as a proper, honest, straightforward man and we, in the best of good faith, appointed him as returning officer; he has made this mistake, or he has committed this error or crime, but we did the best we could and therefore we are not responsible." And they would not be responsible. What responsibility would attach to them? They would say: "We appointed what we believed to be tire best man but he turned out not to be a good man." Therefore what responsibility would attach to the Government?
They would not take any responsibility anyway.

There is no responsibility attaching to them anyway. When my hon. friend the Acting Solicitor General talks about the responsibility resting upon the Government for the selection of the returning officer, he knows as well as I do that the returning and other officers appointed for the purpose of carrying out the next general election will be selected on the recommendation of the Conservative or Unionist candidates. What responsibility attaches to this Government? What responsibility would there be if my hon. friends were returned to power and any question arose as to the proper conduct of a sheriff or any other officer who might be named for conducting the election? They would say: "We did the best we could." What is more liable to happen if my hon. friends appeal to the country than that they shall be sitting on this side of the House and they will say: "It does not make any difference to us whether we appointed the officers or not, you must take the responsibility for their conduct." When my hon. friend talks about the grave responsibility resting upon the Government in appointing these officers, he speaks of something which is a mere myth.



All we want is that proper officers shall be selected and if this amendment were adopted they -would be selected from the officials who are mentioned in the amendment. But in all probability it may not be adopted and my hon. friends will select the returning officers on the advice and recommendation of the Conservative candidates. That is not a fair and proper way to appoint these officials if we are going to do away with patronage. The Acting Solicitor General says that this system has worked well for a number of years. It may be so but when we are adopting a new Franchise Act if we can by making suggestions, in any way assist in getting a fair, reasonable and honest Franchise Act, it is our duty to make those suggestions and to give reasons for them. If this were reversed, if the Liberal party were in power and the time came for an election, I could in my constituency under this Act, if I were so minded, select returning officers and registrars in such a way that, I do not care who might be selected to oppose me, I could win the election. I want to say frankly that I believe that in New Brunswick and throughout the Dominion of Canada governments have not selected such men.

Would the hon. gentleman have any objection to the selection of the officers being left in the hands of the Dominion Alliance, the W.C.T.U. or such moral reform and temperance associations? These are people who, beyond doubt, are not politically appointed.
Do you say that the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) represents them in Parliament?

I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Mackie) would be in a position to suggest that the Dominion Alliance or the W.C.T.U. should select these officers because I do not think he has very much information in regard to the tenets and professions of these organizations. Therefore, I do not think it is worth while taking up the time of the House in discussing that question. These men would be selected by the Liberal or Conservative candidate and if they were so minded the system might result in the selection of men who would leave names off the list that ought to be on it and add names to the list that should not be there, and in that way we would not have a fair or honest election.

Would my hon. friend have any objection to the appointment as 	,
returning officer of some good, intelligent labour man in the city of Moncton?
Not the slightest.
Then why does he want to restrict the Governor in Council?

Because I believe we would not get a labour man selected by the Government in the city of Moncton. We have not in the past had any labour men selected in the city of Moncton as returning officers and I do not think we have had any in the province of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Would my hon. friend have any objection to enlarging the number of persons who might be selected by adding a returned soldier or a member of a city, town or county council or o>f a workingman's union? Is there any reason for excluding such persons from this list?

There is no reason except
that the idea is to keep the selection of returning officers as closely as possible to the line of m n who are more or less responsible to the people so that they know and realize that when they are selected, whether by this 4 p.m. government or a Liberal government, or a local government for those different positions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: By patronage.

Does my hon. friend admit
that the Government are still carrying on patronage?

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend perhaps does not know what I mean. A majority of the officials whom my hon. friend has mentioned have themselves been selected by patronage and what the hon. gentleman desires this House to do is to deprive the Government of the privilege of appointing any others who have been selected by patronage.

My hon. friend is entirely
wrong.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why?
In saying that they are appointed by patronage. They are not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who, for instance?

The sheriff of the city of *
St. John and the municipal clerks and secretary-treasurers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
How does my hon.
friend know by what influence the city clerk or any other officer of a municipal council was elected or appointed? What

right have you to say that the means by which that gentleman might be selected are any more proper than the means by which this returning officer would be selected by the Government?

Would the hon. gentleman
say that the clerk in the town from which he comes was selected by political patronage?	~

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
This government is
as much entitled, and is just as liable, to make an appointment that is proper as an *officer appointed by a city or town council.

My hon. friend has shifted
his ground again.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Not at all.

My hon. friend cannot get
around it by asking any such question as that. I will ask the hon. gentleman if any [customs house officer, postmaster, sheriff, city or town clerk or municipal secretary-treasurer in his constituency would not be a fair and reasonable man to hold an election.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have not said he was not.
Don't you admit that he is?

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
My argument does
not proceed upon that basis. I contend that selection can be made under this clause of a man who is just as good and just as able to perform the service required as any other official.

That part I will admit at
once. But my hon. friend is not prepared to say that any one of the officials named in the proposed amendment would not be admirably fitted to conduct an election in his own riding. What he does say is this: " No, we won't accept any of those men, but w'e will accept a man that I may recommend to the Government to be my returning officer."

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have not said anything of the kind. On the contrary I believe we can make a very proper selection from any of the officials mentioned.
Then you ought to support the amendment.	.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No. I say we have the right to-day, and perhaps in some cases we would make our selection from among such officials, but we do not want to be compelled to do so.
No, because my hon. friend wants to nominate the returning officer in his own riding.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That is perfectly
right because then I have the responsibility.

I have already spoken on this subject and I have no desire to repeat myself. I rise only to point out to my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) that nine-tenths of the very eloquent speech he made a few minutes ago is based upon an entire misapprehension of this amendment. I say "misapprehension" because I , know my hon. friend too well to assume that he would intentionally misrepresent me. Again and again he said: Under this amendment we are willing to trust an official appointed by the Provincial Governments, but we are not willing to trust an official appointed by the Federal Government. My hon. friend is entirely wrong. This list contains a number of officials who receive their appointments from the Government at Ottawa, and I think I am safe in stating that although in West Elgin probably half a dozen of the class of officials enumerated in that list have been appointed by the hon. gentleman himself, yet we are willing to trust them. So when he says we will trust only men appointed by the local governments my hon. friend is entirely wrong.
I did not say "only."

I have listened with attention to my esteemed friend, the exMinister of Labour (Mr. Crothers), as I do every time he rises in fhis House, and I am led to believe that in regard to appointments made by the Provincial Governments my hon. friend has forgotten one essential thing-that since 1911 appointments of the class of officers enumerated in the amendment have been made exclusively by the Conservative party, and that probably there is scarcely a collector of customs-

Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me one word in reply to the Te, marks he has just made, as well as to those recently made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). In speaking about the Opposition being unwilling to trust any man appointed by this Government, I had no reference at all to the officers now operating under this Government, such as postmasters, collectors of customs, collectors of inland revenue, and so on; I was referring to men that this Government might appoint from this time forward as returning officers under this Act	,

This amendment enables the Government to make their appointments from among customs officers, and, practically speaking, every one of them now holding office is an appointee of the present Government. Therefore we are not partial in respect to the class of men to be appointed. The same remark applies to postmasters-there is scarcely a postmaster who has not been appointed by the present Government. Therefore the Government will find that they have all their appointees since 1911 from whom to select returning officers. But there is another reason why I am so strongly in favour of this amendment. The hon. member for Kent county (Mr. Leger) said he wanted to see men of responsibility appointed as returning officers. By this amendment the Government is in a position to appoint men as returning officers from among a thoroughly responsible and substantial class, for the officials mentioned in the amendment are men who have won the respect of the community by the faithful discharge of their duties, and therefore it may be safely assumed that they will so act as returning officers that their reputation will not suffer, for they cannot leave the country if they have done something of a questionable character at an election.
That is .the point.

They are men who are held in the highest respect by the community, and in the interests of themselves and their families they must so act as to preserve that respect. So the Government is sure to have the right class of men appointed as returning officers. These men have by the faithful discharge of their duty gained the respect and esteem of the community, and they may be trusted to do nothing to injure their reputation.

Does the hon. member insinuate that a candidate would select a "high binder" as a returning officer, who would leave the country after the election? _
Mr. TUEljJiON: Not at all; but mistakes are made by the most honourable men in the selection of appointees.
Even by ministers of the Crown.

Yes. I do not say that they would, do it dishonestly, but such mistakes may be made. The reputation of these officials is the best guarantee for the proper discharge of their duties as returning officers, and I believe this amendment

is broad enough to give us not only officials appointed by the Federal Government, but officials holding their appointments from the provincial and municipal authorities. Therefore I hope and trust that the minister will accept the suggestion contained in this amendment.

This is an Act which is applicable to the whole Dominion, but up to the present the discussion has been confined largely to hon. gentlemen representing constituencies in the eastern and central portions of the country. In so far as the amendment is applicable to the West, I would say that it is unworkable. There is no guarantee or assurance that the persons named will be available for this service; that in many western constituencies they will be found at all. In fact, I can mention constituencies in which none of the persons named are to be found. One of these is West Edmonton.

Is my hon. friend not
aware that the amendment provides that if none of the officials named are available the Government may nominate whomever they please?

That is just the point I am coming to. In many Western constituencies these officials named in the amendment cannot be found. In any case, I rather think that the municipalities who employ them will not always be ready to consent that they shall be taken from their service for two or three months for the purpose of conducting an election. If the amendment is to have any value at all, a large number of officials will have to be added to that list,-so large a number, in fact, that you will be getting back to precisely the effect of the Bill as it now stands.

Surely my hon. friend
has failed to read the amendment. If these officials cannot be found; if they refuse to serve; if their employers will not allow them to accept appointments,-if any of these "ifs" happen, then the Governor in Council may appoint any competent man. My hon. friend's argument, therefore, is based on a misapprehension.
Therefore the amendment is quite unnecessary.

That is quite different from the view my hon. friend expressed a moment ago-that the amendment is unworkable. It is perfectly workable. If any of these officials can be found; well and good. If not, the Government have 'a. free hand. What more can be asked?

The effect of the
amendment is to have a state of affairs prevailing in one part of Canada which does not prevail elsewhere, whereas the Bill is intended to apply to the whole of Canada.

The Bill applies to the whole of Canada, hut what my hon. friend describes as possible in one place is equally possible in another. In a large city-Montreal, for example-there are many constituencies, and so many returning officers are needed that it may not be possible to obtain them all from this list. The condition applying to West Edmonton may apply anywhere, and this amendment fully covers it.

I am sure it is the
feeling of hon. gentlemen who have spoken that the law should be administered in a way that is fair to all. I have a proposal to make which, I believe, if agreed to by the Government and by the Opposition, would be in the best interests of all concerned and would give no advantage to either the iGovernment or the Opposition. I suggest that in each constituency, wherever possible-and I believe it would be possible in ninety per cent of the constituencies- the returning officers be selected from among those who have become identified with and are supporters of the new national policy. Under that arrangement neither Government nor the Opposition would get any advantage, and the law would be fairly administered.
Mr. Chairman-

May I put a question
to my hon. friend (Mr. Johnston)?

Order. Mr. Power
has the floor.

Is the new party a
political party?

It is a movement, not
a party.

As I understand it, the
Acting Solicitor General argues that these officials have been appointed in* this way for the last fifty years and that the system has worked well.
Except in 1917.

It may be true that we
have had this system for the last fifty years, and it may or may not have worked well. But in the short time during which I have been interested in politics and in the organizations of elections I have found that invariably the first thing done by the
political organization is to endeavour to obtain control of the nomination of the election officers. Now, if this were not important to the political party which is organizing for an election, I hardly think that they would go to the trouble that they do. If we cannot go so far as to say that under the arrangement proposed by the Bill, "the cards are stacked,''we can at least say, in the gambling parlance, that there is " a large percentage in favour of the house ''-the house in this case being the Government. There 'will be such a percentage if the Government aTe allowed to name something like 22,000 henchmen and political heelers all over the country. My short experience in elections has taught me this, too:	That in the large number of cases
the men appointed as returning officers are the men whom the candidate thinks he can use for his own purposes and his own advantage. I have come to the conclusion after studying this matter for some time, and I have no doubt that it is the experience of most other hon. members, though they do not not want to say so. Now, if these election officers are appointed by a prominent official, an official who has some responsibility, the result is apt to be more satisfactory. The returning officer should be a man respected by the community. If he is selected from the list suggested by the amendment, we have some guarantee that he is an honest man; we have some guarantee that he will exercise his functions in a fair and impartial manner. Under the provision as proposed, our only safeguard is the honesty of the candidate supporting the Government, or-I do not wish to impugn the honesty of any hon. gentleman opposite, but this is most likely to be our only safeguard-the honesty of the political henchmen of the candidate; the honesty of whoever happens to be the head of the political organization. In all elections, with the exception, perhaps, of those held by the saintly gentlemen mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Griesbach), the Dominion Alliance and others, there is a certain amount of evasion of the law. The candidate, as a rule, does not wish to know of these evasions, so he leaves the matter to his more discreet partisans, and his discreet partisans, if they can thereby give some degree of favour to their candidate, appoint only those men who are willing to extend that favour. Under the circumstances, it is only fair and reasonable that the amendment should carry.
As to the question of responsibility, the officials named in the amendment are re-

sponsible men; they are respected by the community, otherwise they would not have remained in the positions which they occupy. But in any case, our experience since the last election has been that the .Government have refused to accept responsibility for the acts of their agents. We have heard of ballot boxes being stuffed; of the overseas soldiers' votes being switched from one county to another; of hundreds of votes being given in constituencies where they should not have been given; of soldiers being forced to vote under the threat [DOT]of being sent back to the front line trenches. We have heard all this time and again in this House since the last election, and I do not wish to go into it again. The Government have refused to take the responsibility, saying: What the soldiers want, we want, and the soldiers have done well by putting the Government in power and we have done well by the soldiers; therefore, if there was corruption, even if there had been in this election something that was illegal, we were perfectly right and we accept the full responsibility because the soldiers did it, and we encouraged then:. That is to say, because the soldiers did wrong and because we did wrong ip encouraging the soldiers, everything was all right.. Therefore, any government could do that, and the next time this may not be for the soldiers; it may be that the Government will say: We have allowed the farmers to do it. Therefore, the thing may be quite right, because the farmers of the soil were in favour of it. I maintain, as I have said before, that when we go into this question, we should see to it that "the pei-centage is not in favour of the house," that we have a fair and square deal. We do net ask for any favours. We know as well as most members of this House know that the life of this Government is but of short duration.
The shorter the better.

We are quite sure that hon. gentlemen opposite will not have to assume this responsibility after the next election. Therefore, we ask them to accept this amendment for their own sake, because they maay be out of power for a long time.
Mr. GRIESBAiCH: The hon. gentleman does not believe that 'this proposal will be as efficacious as he said a moment ago that it would be. He seems to be quite sure that it will not be needed.
I do not quite understand the hon. gentleman. Will he repeat his remarks?
If I have to explain-
Just repeat; we could not hear on this side.

The hon. gentleman, first of all, begins by saying that the present proposal, using his language, which is not familiar to me, I may say, gives "the percentage to the house," suggesting that the advantage will all be with the Government, and then he proceeds to say that as a result of the election held, I assume, in accordance with this Bill, this Government will disappear.
Not under this Bill. You may steal it under the Bill as you did last time.

I am under the impression -and I think the country is with me-when I say that nothing can possibly be done by this Government to save it from the disaster which is about to overtake it. We have been told that the list contained in the amendment is so long that we might add any one else, the labour man, the returned soldier, any class of citizen in the community. That is quite true, but the officials named in the amendment are all officials who have some standing in the community, who are responsible to the community for their good conduct.
They are all under bond.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are not under bond to this Government.
That makes no difference.

We care little about their responsibility to this Government, but we care a great deal about their responsibility to the people of Canada, and these officials are already responsible to the people of Canada in that if they commit an illegal act, there is a penalty attached to that. Under the circumstances, I think the Acting Solicitor General ought to accept the amendment of my hon. friend.

I take it that the purpose of the amendment moved by the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) is that the selection of returning officers must be made from men of repute in the community, and he enumerates a list of supposedly reputable men holding certain positions in a constituency. I am not going to criticise or say that these men whom he enumerates are not respectable and reputable citizens in a great

many portions of Canada. But as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Gries-bach) has said, this is not a Bill for Nova Scotia or Quebec; this is a Bill for the Dominion of Canada. And when you say that you must preferably, as I would assume from the discussion, select a returning officer from amongst the sheriffs, that may apply in Nova Scotia, Quebec, or even Ontario; but what happens when you get into Western Canada? We have possibly two or three sheriffs in the whole province of Alberta; the Edmonton district to-day has not a sheriff at all. We have possibly two registrars of deeds in the whole province, .men whose duties are so arduous that every minute of their time is occupied, so that they could not perform the duties of returning officer. As regards collectors of customs, we have in probably the four largest cities of Alberta men who are holding the position of collector of customs, who are reputable, responsible citizens, occupying an exalted position, drawing possibly a large remuneration; but the duties of those men are so arduous that it would be impossible for them to leave their duties in order to take two or two and a half months to perform the duties of returning officer in a constituency. As regards the postmasters, if you take a postmaster in a small community away from a large city, you have a man drawing the magnificent salary of possibly $35 a year, and he does not necessarily have to be a man of repute in his community. The trouble is to find men to keep post offices in Western Canada; indeed, men are almost urged to accept the positions, and it does not follow that they are the most reputable men in the community. As regards secretaries of municipalities, we do not have municipalities in Alberta except in a very few instances; we have secretaries of local improvement districts who get, perhaps, $200 or $300 a year from that position. It does not follow that a man occupying that position is the prominent citizen that we have heard spoken of here to-day, who should be charged with the duty of acting as returning officer in a constituency. We could select almost any one outside of that list, and we would have better men than those who are enumerated in that list. The hon. gentleman provides for that. He says: If you cannot select them from that list, we shall allow you to select them from some other people. Eor my part, I think the clause as it is now is quite satisfactory and permits us to select the best men for the position of returning officer in a constituency. I have had some extended experience in political life now, and I have yet to hear of one case where a returning officer violated the vows of his office and committed fraudulent acts, and I doubt very much if there are many cases in the whole Dominion of Canada where a finger could be pointed at any act which has been performed by any returning officer.

I want to point out what appear to me to be discrepancies in the views put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite. Yesterday afternoon and this afternoon also, we heard them stating over and over again first that the Government had to assume the responsibility, and then the list as now submitted is a list that is too narrow, that will not allow the Government to choose at leisure or properly the particular person who shall be named returning officer. I am sorry hon. members opposite do not more often read the very interesting speeches delivered in this House by the Acting Prime Minister !(Sir George Foster).
I always make a point of listening carefully to what the Acting Prime Minister says, and of even reading his speeches in Hansard. This is what he said yesterday afternoon, in direct contradiction, I submit, of the two points submitted by our friends on the other side, namely, that we are trying to take the responsibility away from the Government, and secondly, that our list i? too narrow. This is what he said:
My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) has given^ a list of certain officials within the range of which shall be limited the choice of returning officers by whatever government is in power and is directing the election. As I read the amendment, any one of eight, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty or thirty different persons may be chosen by the Government as returning officer; the list is a pretty generous one. The reason for proposing that limitation is that a government may start out with the idea of using influence which it ought not to use by choosing as returning officers men of their own political belief. Well, if the Government really sets out with that idea in mind, to what extent is th* carrying out of that intention limited by r<-stricting appointments as returning officers to a list of twenty or thirty officials? It will be Quite possible for a malevolently-minded government to select from that list at least one person from each electoral district who may or can carry on its nefarious designs. The amendment, therefore, is nothing more or less than camouflage. The whole thing depends on whether the Government does set out with the idea of using its returning officers for wrong and evil purposes.
The Acting Prime Minister could not have made it more plain that the Government will have full responsibility for nominations under this amendment. The Government will still have the power of nomination

in their hands, and if they choose to do wrong they can do so.

Does my hon. friend
agree with the sentiments he has just quoted?
I do and I do not.

Oh, oh.
i	[DOT] If hon. members who are
laughing had had more experience they would know that it is very seldom that a v/itness, and I am now in the witness box, answers a question simply by Yes or No! There are many questions which a man cannot answer in that way. I asked a ques-*>on of the Minister of Justice last night, *o which he could not give me a Yes or No answer, because it was impossible. So my hon. friend need not think he has scored such a big success, because I did not answer Yes or No to his question. My answer is that the Acting Prime Minister is absolutely right when he says that if this Government wants to perpetrate any wrong in an election they can do it under this amendment, for the list is wide, but, remember, it takes two in this particular case to commit a wrong-the Government and the official who receives the nomination. Under this amendment the Government could appoint only responsible officials, who would not forfeit their position or their honour under any considerations, I believe. Under the present system -I am not saying that it is done, but it can be-the Government may appoint whoever they like; they may appoint a person who is absolutely unworthy. I do not think they would do that intentionally, but they might be misled into doing it by the partisans in the particular constituency concerned. We know how these things are done. It has already been explained to this committee. Partisans in a constituency gather together and submit to the Government the name of an official for returning officer. They say to themselves:	Here is
our man. If we get him appointed, we shall have the nomination of the deputy returning officers, and of all the registrars, clerks, and so on. Do they &do that with the intention of stealing the election, and of committing a fraud? Not generally, but that might happen some times. In nearly every case it is done with the intention of getting the patronage in these appointments. When the returning officer has been appointed, he knows that it is due to this committee or the candidate, and the next step is for the committee or for the candidate to approach him and 
say: I would like Mr. So-and-so appointed deputy returning officer. More than that, they hand the returning officer a list of the men they want appointed as registrars, clerks, and so on. Some one might ask, do you think the returning officer would lend himself to such a practice as that and appoint whoever the candidate or the committee recommends? Well, it has been done in a great many constituencies.
Where?
In my constituency, in the next constituency to it, in three-quarters of the constituencies of Canada in the last general election.
Do you know what you are talking about?
It was done not with a view to committing electoral fraud, but with a view to distributing the patronage.
And winning the election.
It may have been so in some cases, but I am not going so far as to say that.
Does the hon. member know anything at all about the conditions in the province of Ontario, for instance, or is he speaking of a province with which he is more familiar?

I am speaking from the knowledge which I gathered generally during the last Dominion election, and afterwards, in this House, Where the frauds which were committed were denounced - time and again. The hon. member knows perfectly well that in the last general election, frauds of the worst possible kind were perpetrated. He must remember the discussions we had in this House. But even if I had not been in this country at the last general election, if I had been in Europe I would know enough to say what I am saying now with respect to this system of patronage which has existed for the last fifty years in the nomination of these officials.
I am not speaking of any wrong-doing, but simply of patronage. I say that this' system of patronage which has existed for the last fifty years was continued at the last general election. It goes on more or less all the time. Now we want to stop that. We want to prevent a set of men who are working for a certain candidate from securing the nomination of a returning officer and handing him a list of the registrars and clerks he shall appoint throughout the constituency.

Would my hon. friend believe in restricting the returning officer in the selection of his deputies by some such scheme as the amendment proposes, or would he give the returning officer a free hand in that matter?

I would give him a free hand, although this may be subject to discussion from a different point of view. The amendment leaves absolute discretion to the returning officer in the appointment of his assistants. I know that in the province of Quebec, where a Liberal Government has been in power since 1897, the officials who are chosen as returning officers are sheriffs, prothonotaries, or registrars of deeds, and these officers make it a point to consult both candidates. My hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) smiles, but it is true. I can testify to that. It has been done in every election in every constituency in the province of Quebec.
Men who occupy public offices of importance, and by reason of which they have an enviable standing in 'their communities, have too great a sense of responsibility, not only to the public but to themselves, to think for a moment of favouring one party or the other, or of giving undue advantage to either. Their sense of fair play compels them to consult both sides, and as a matter of personal experience I know that time and again they have communicated with representatives of both parties and have nominated the deputy returning officers, clerks, etc., from both sides. I am not aware that thiis was done in the last federal election. However, I think that I 'have said sufficient to dispose of the contention that registrars, prothonotaries, etc., must still be partisans merely by reason of the fact that they happened to be appointed by a partisan government some years ago. I have sufficient faith in the honesty of men who hold such high and important positions to spurn the suggestion that they would allow their previous political affiliations and cieeds to influence them to the extent of bestowing patronage entirely on one party to the disadvantage of the other. I do not believe that they would do such a thing, and I know that in the province of Quebec they unquestionably do not. But apart from every other consideration, would we not be more secure in the nomination of these men than in the nomination of some man or other whom this Government, without any possible knowledge of local circumstances, might be advised to appoint? I want it distinctly understood, as I have said, that I impute no improper
motives or intentions to the Government, for I do not think for a moment that the Government would deliberately nominate any man whom they knew to be unworthy. But surely the Government must see that they cannot possibly consider all the circumstances that should weigh in the nomination of these men. The Government cannot possibly find time to go into the minutiae, to study the.'peculiar conditions in every corner of the country, and so to acquaint themselves with the circumstances as to be able to take the necessary precautions in order that their nominations may be perfectly just and impartial. I say that they cannot do that. They have to rely upon some one in the constituency whose advice they have to take. If their adviser happens to be a straightforward and honest man the nominations will be just. But if he happens to be crooked there is no hope of fair play. It was said a moment ago by some hon. gentlemen that if a returning officer were found to be guilty under this Act he could be brought before the proper tribunal, but it was also pointed out that he could very well leave the country after the election, and it does not require much argument to show that a man who is not responsible to the public but is only temporarily resident in any district can easily escape the consequences of any misconduct on his part. He might perpetrate any sort of fraud while the election was on, and might completely wreck an election in some particular constituency, and the moment the election was over he could skip out of the country. Of course, this is a hypothetical case of abnormal character, and I do not at all base my argument on it. But I mention it to show the extent to which things may go. On the other hand, if you select a man who has a recognized standing in the community and who is jealous of his good name, you have every chance of justice and fair play, and you may depend upon it that he will try to act fairly as between the parties. Suppose in any constituency any candidate should approach such a man and address him in this manner:	"You know
that I was the sitting member before the . House dissolved, and I should be glad if you would make certain nominations which I shall suggest to you." What would happen? This officer would not say: "I have no business with you, Mr. Candidate; I don't care to speak with you; you had better go home." In such a case the candidate would be of course helpless. But if you hkd some irresponsible man appointed to the office, material influence might easily be brought

to bear upon him, and it is not difficult to imagine what might pass between the two.

Does the hon. member
think that it is proper for a candidate to interfere with an officer in such a manner?
Well, we all try to get some nominations made in our favour. Did not the hon. gentleman himself interfere in the last election?
No.
Oh, no, I suppose not.
I agree with the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment in the desire to have nothing to say as a member about these matters.

If my hon. friend did not interview the officer personally he must be an exception, because we know that these things are done. Where two or three hundred people are being nominated it is but natural that both sides should desire to see that the nominations are made as fairly as possible. I do not say that the hon. gentleman interfered. There may not have been any interference in his case, and I give him the benefit of the doubt; but in nine cases out of ten we know that this is done, and there is no use in being hypocritical about it.

Does the hon. member impute hypocrisy both to myself and to the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) ? We both declared our intention to have nothing to do with the appointing of these people.

My hon. friend apparently cannot understand that I am not casting any aspersions on him nor am I alluding to him when I say that we should frankly admit what is a matter of common knowledge, and not indulge in any hypocritical pretensions. I am not speaking of the hon. gentleman in particular or of any one else in this chamber, but I say that there is no use in denying the fact to which I have referred. If in the last election or any other election the hon. gentleman was simply a phlegmatic spectator, coolly looking on and caring not whether this man or the other was appointed deputy returning officer, or how trwo or three hundred nominations were made, I give him credit .for being an unnatural exception to what is undoubtedly a general rule. No hon. gentleman in this House will pretend for a moment that both sides are not anxious to have these nominations fairly made. No one will seriously suggest, I think, that

it does not .make a very substantial difference as to how these two or three hundred persons who exercise an important influence on the final results, are disposed of; nor will any one pretend that it would not be a mighty advantage to the party who could secure their appointment to suit themselves. To come back to the point from which I was distracted by imy hon. friend. This amendment is wide enough to enable the Government to choose competent men who will have enough time to devote to the positions to which they are appointed. The amendment is wide and broad enough to allow the Government to assume the full responsibility for the nomination. Under these circumstances, until my hon. friends on the other side have answered the arguments brought forward yesterday afternoon by the right hon. the Acting Prime Minister, I submit that our contention should be upheld.

As I understand it, the mover of the amendment aims at getting rid of partisanship in the conduct of elections. In reading the remarks he made yesterday I could not see that any case had been made out against the existing system, that there had been any rank cases of partisanship in the conduct of our elections or that the new system proposed would improve the old. The government that would be in power would have the opportunity of selecting under this amendment a great many men who might still be extreme partisans. They are not compelled to select a sheriff or a registrar. They can select the secretary-treasurer of a municipality, as I read it, and, taking my own constituency, there would be a large number of men of that type from whom they could select. You could very easily get a man who would be just as extreme a partisan in an election under any such system. If the intention was to go and find men who might be improperly influenced, under this amendment, it is possible to get men of that kind. In all the elections I have contested I have had the responsibility of naming the returning officer. I am on fairly good terms with my political opponents and I have never heard any of them complain of the action of the returning officer who was appointed. I think the average member of Parliament is anxious to place in that position a man who will conduct the business honourably and uprightly so that there will be no criticism directed against himself personally. I think that is the ambition of the average member of Par-

liament. I do not think that we can improve the existing system by this amendment. If a man is determined that he is going to have a partisan as a returning officer he can get him under this amendment because there are plenty of opportunities to get a man of that type.
Reference has been made to the conditions in Western Canada. I will be local in my remarks because I can deal with the situation a little better from the local standpoint being familiar with the conditions there. The sheriff for the judicial district of Lethbridge has no assistant. If he were appointed a. returning officer he would have to give all his time to the position and there is no one to do his work as sheriff. Mention is made of the registrar. In Alberta there are only two registrars, one located in Calgary and the other in Edmonton. In the balance of the constituencies it is impossible to select a -registrar. Then we come to the secretary-treasurer of a city, incorporated town or municipality. That would give an opportunity for the selection of men who were still interested in politics and who were identified with one or the other of the political parties. I imagine that under an amendment of this nature a man who Was a partisan would probably select one of the municipal officers because there would be just as much danger of partisanship in a selection of that kind as under the existing system. I am as anxious as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) to remove all danger of corruption and dishonesty in connection with our elections but I do not think that a case has been made out to 5 p.m. show that the existing system is so bad that it can be improved by the adoption of this amendment. That is my view after having read the debate which took place yesterday and after having heard some of the remarks which have been made to-day.

We are not all as fortunate as the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) who need not care very much which party is in power because he is always with the party in power. Consequently, he need not fear the result of any appointment. Some of us have the habit of staying on our own side of politics and must submit to the fortunes of our party. For that reason we desire to see that proper care is taken in the appointment of officials to handle serious business of this kind bn behalf of the people. When the old conditions were in vogue the returning officer
had nothing to do as his functions were purely administrative. He simply had to do certain things which were laid down for him but the present conditions are entirely different. The officer whom we are taking power to appoint makes the list. That was not so under the old conditions. In our province the lists were made by the officials of the municipality appointed and entirely under, municipal control. Even the Provincial Government in our province had nothing to do with the lists. The councils in the different municipalities appoint the officers to deal with the lists and the local government have nothing to do with the lists upon which they run their own elections. Consequently there is no partisanship because in our province the councillors do not all belong to the same political parties and whatever the complexion of the council may be the councillors appoint their own officers.
May I say to the hon. gentleman: Except in Halifax?

I would not say that nothing good ever comes out of Halifax. Sometimes the councillors in Halifax have a way of doing their own business. I have heard no complaint. What my hon. friend says may be so in Halifax but in the part of the province from which I come the majority of the council of the county of Cape Breton has been Liberal for many years and the councillors who are not supporting the majority have the selection of their own [DOT] officials and in that way control the making of the lists. I wish to say to the right hon. the leader of the Government, because he and the Government are responsible for the view they take of this subject, that they cannot reasonably take shelter behind the old conditions. As I have pointed out, the duties of the officials under the old system were simply of a mechanical character so to speak but now a change has taken place by Vhich the party in power have taken the list under their own control and they are selecting the jury, empannelling them and taking away the right even of objecting to any of the persons called to serve upon that jury. They are appointing their own officials and taking the whole machinery into their own hands. I wish to remind the leader of the Government that there are a great many charges against this Government, some of them right and some of them wrong.
Very few wrong.

I think the Government generally have reason to believe that they will have a pretty hard proposition when they go to the country lor re-election. Therefore I would advise them not to further weaken the reputation of the Conservative party, or the Union party, as the case may be, by trying to once more create a machine to insure their return to power. In the early stages of this discussion we had a statement from the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Mackie), I think it was, which is very significant. He said: "If we try once more to get ourselves back to power we will certainly do so and so in connection with this legislation." That would imply, it seems to me, that once before they created machinery to get them back to power. The question now arises: Will they try it once more? I would advise my hon. friend and the Government that it will be the part of wisdom for them not to place this further blot on the reputation of the party by making the attempt, which in my judgment will be absolutely futile and will add to the difficulties oi those who may come after them as their lineal descendants.
I am in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). I think it gives sufficient scope for the Government to exercise their judgment in getting proper men as returning officers, and it at least gives them an opportunity to select men of the very highest integrity from among the officials enumerated. The people of this country realize that a man holding the position of customs officer, postmaster, sheriff, or municipal secretary-treasurer is of some standing in the community, and I venture to say that -no reflection at all will he cast upon the Government if they select men of that stamp as returning officers. I am surprised that hon. gentlemen opposite are objecting to the adoption of the wise plan suggested by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, and I hope that on maturer consideration the leader of the Government will advise acceptance of the amendment.

I have only two or three words to add to this discussion. It seems to me that a little story I have heard -in the West is quite appropriate at this time. A man was asked if he was well-acquainted with three prevaricators in the locality and he replied: "Yes. Dick Smith is one; Tom Jones is the other two." Now, it strikes me that in connection with this amendment hon. gentlemen have so often repeated and

re-hashed their argument that they have actually come to believe it themselves. The amendment is based on wrong premises. It presumably ennunciates the opinion that ability, integrity and every other good quality are centered in the class of officials referred to. Now, that is not so. I can cite instances where many officials of the class mentioned have been deposed because of crookedness. I can give a longer list than any that has been given in the House today of wrong-doings by returning officers. Although I have perhaps but a very limited political experience in the West, I -can cite instances and produce proof of many wrong acts by such men. One instance I might mention: Mr. Turgeon, a minister in the Saskatchewan Government, who is the son of the hon. member, for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) has several times had occasion to depose individuals of the class mentioned in this list. Speaking of customs officers, for instance, that is one class of individual in this country that I oppose more than any other, because I cannot see on what premises it can be argued that they are absolutely honest and trustworthy. If I had my records here I could cite cases where men of this class have wilfully imposed on people in a way that the law certainly does not sanction, and I cannot see why this amendment should recommend that class of officials for appointment as returning officers. A few moments ago an hon. gentleman on the opposite side of the House said that a lot of men in the post offices in the West would not have his recommendation as men of honesty and integrity. Those men are not appointed because they alone possess those qualities, and to assume that they are the only people fit to act as returning officers is, inferentially, a condemnation of others who do not hold such appointments. I argue that the Government be consistent in the attitude they have taken in respect to this Bill, especially if they take into consideration the record of past elections. I intend to support the clause as presented by the Government as I feel that it is the only and right and proper thing to do.

I notice that section 22 empowers the Governor in -Council to appoint returning officers. I would like to ask the hon. Acting Solicitor General if the Governor in Council is a political body; if so, I think the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) is quite right and should be accepted by the Government. We want politics taken out of this Bill, and we

had a promise from the hon. minister that that would be done. I am sure that he is not ready to state that many members of the Cabinet are not partisans. Therefore it is high time we should look narrowly into this section and see if its defects will not be remedied by the adoption of this amendment.
In regard to the class of officials enumerated in the amendment, I 'beg to state, in reply to some of my hon. friends on the other side of the House, that returned soldiers are at the present time occupying .many such positions, namely, as collectors of customs, postmasters, and -so on; consequently, there is no danger that our friends, the returned soldiers, will not have an opportunity to act as returning officers. As far as postmasters are concerned, I venture to say that in my own constituency at least one-half of them are farmers; therefore that particular- class will be represented. With regard to clerks of the peace and municipal secretary-treasurers, I have had some opportunities of studying the appointments to these positions in my own province, and I find that as a rule such appointments are made for a certain time, and on failure to discharge their duties faithfully and honestly the appointees are liable to dismissal at any moment. All men occupying such positions in my own province are looked upon as good reliable men, and therefore I feel assured that the proper conduct of elections will be safeguarded if returning officers are appointed from among these officials.
As a rule the sheriffs all through the eastern part of Canada have always given satisfactory service. I know of only one case in New Brunswick where a sheriff failed to do his duty, buit the candidate who had the majority of the votes did not suffer, being declared duly elected by the court. I will not go into the details, but there was some mistake with Tegard to the posting of the proclamation and as to the date for the receiving of the reports of the returning officer. In my opinion the sheriff is in a position to give ample satisfaction as returning officer. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I support the amendment.

I wish to join with
