hon. members on this side in supporting the amendment presented by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding). T think that hon. members on both sides agree in their desire to have a fair franchise law and to create machinery for the holding of honest elections in the future-for at last election
things were not done as some people thought they should be. We want to prevent that at the next election, and this amendment will tend to prevent wrongdoing. It proposes that returning officers shall be selected from certain officials in the towns, cities and municipalities who may be regarded as the best men to give satisfactory service, and against whom no reflection can be made. In the last election a prominent notary in my constituency was suggested as returning officer. Unfortunately, there was another man in the county, a bailiff, of the same name-Cimon, and he was selected to be the returning officer. So that instead of having a man who was centrally located and had a permanent office or place of business, we had this bailiff, who was travelling about the constituency serving summonses and orders and rules of the court. Two days before polling day I was informed that some boxes had not been provided for certain polling stations. We tried to communicate with the returning officer, but we could not fine him; whereas if he had a place of residence or place of business which was well known >-and that idea is incorporated in my hon. friend's amendment-there would have been no difficulty in finding him and in having this matter attended to. The officials enumerated in the amendment would be men of long experience in public life, in political affairs, in certain professions and callings; they would all have the experience required of persons who should fulfil the duties of returning officer. Further, they have the confidence of all the people; otherwise they would not occupy these positions. These conditions would not apply to bailiffs, insurance agents, or any Tom, Dick or Harry whom the Government might appoint upon the recommendation of their candidates. I do not see what harm there would be in incorporating in this clause the amendment of my hon. friend; it is merely an assurance that the recurrence of irregularities will be prevented. For these reasons, I shall vote for the amendment,,

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice):
speechtext:
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, before the question is put, I would like to say a few words to the committee on the amendment of the hen. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). We know that the country has just been through a most trying period. There is evidence that distrust, even hate, is rampant in our land. Even in this House accusations have been hurled at the Admin-

istration concerning the elections held in 1917. The right honourable, the Acting Prime Minister told us, a few days ago, that we should have done with these bitter quarrelings in Parliament; it was high time, he said, that we began to trust one another. Well, Mr. iSpeaker, if the Government, in their heart and soul, really do wish to bring about this spirit of harmony, they could ask for no better opportunity of proving it than the one afforded by the present discussion of the Franchise Act which we are about to bestow upon the country.
I am well aware that this legislation applies to the country as a whole, and my Western friends, of the National Progressive party, are telling me nothing new when they say that this Act is as much concerned with the West as with the East. This is not a question of patronage. The hon. Minister of Milita (Mr. Guthrie) contends that we should keep up that' system, because it has shown itself to he workable. But he is oblivious of the fact that conditions are not the same and that he cannot invoke as a precedent that happened prior to 1917, nor what has happened since that date. I may lay claim to the honour of representing a constituency in this House since 1900; I have had the pleasant, or unpleasant experience, of going through six elections-I should say the pleasant experience, since I won them all-following hard-fought contests. On each occasion the returning officer appointed by the Government was either the county registrar or the prothonotary of the Superior *Court, with the sole exception of 1917. However, it was pointed out by one of the hon. members who preceded me, we must not lose sight of the fact that, prior to 1917, the voters' list was drawn up by the officers of the municipality and revised by a tribunal appointed, in some cases-, by the Provincial Government and, I believe, by the municipality itself, in the cities of Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers, Hull and Sherbrooke, Once the list was completed and revised those whose names did not appear were not entitled to vote. Nobody could come along and say; such and such a name must be put on the list; such and such a name must be scratched off. Moreover, as I said a moment ago, these officers, for the most part, were chosen amongst those named in the amendment moved -by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's; and the reason for this was 
explained by one of the hon. members who preceded me.
. The task before us is not only to stamp out the patronage evil but to re-establish public confidence in the efficiency of parliamentary government and prove to the people of this country that Parliament has not forsaken dignity, that governments still have some respect for the representatives of the people who come to sit in this House. We must prove our good faith and we could find no better way of doing so than by accepting the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. Why so? Because in every county the registrar, the sheriff, the town clerk or any of the other officers mentioned, are men whom the people trust, men who must furnish a bond to the corporation or the legislature, whichever authority appoints them, as a guarantee of faithful adherence to duty. But, says the hon. Minister of Militia, they are not under bond to this Government. Whoever has the slightest acquaintance with the subject, whoever wants to use his judgment, will readily understand that a public servant who is under a bond to fulfil his duty towards one and all has no inducement to act in such a way as to destroy the confidence of those who believe in him. Therefore public opinion, if not the opinion of this Government and this House, holds that such a man will prove more faithful in the accomplishment of his duty than the man who is appointed for the time being only and who is under no necessity to retain the confidence of the public; who, once the election over, disappears from the scene and retires to private life, gnd who entertains the hope that whatever he may do to improve his own situation during the short time that the elections do last, is fraught with no consequences to himself, other than political, and that he will never be called upon by his fellow-citizens to give an account of his conduct.
After all, we must take things as we find them. Why, during a debate in this House last year we were met with smiles when we stated that the election had not been held in an honest, fair and impartial way; we were even told: What we did was a very creditable thing, since we did it to gain our end and the end justifies the means. We decidedly cannot expect the public to have much confidence in a parliament which proclaims the doctrine that the end justifies the means. And when we endeavoured to show by specific instances how unfairly and unjustly election work

had been carried on; when we requested the Government and the House to appoint a board of enquiry so that they might reveal, in all their hideousness, these specific instances of agrant dishonesty on the part of the Government, had the door brutally slammed in their faces. I say brutally because the Government practically admitted the accusations, but their answer was: We snap our fingers in your faces. We had an end to gain; we have gained that end-, so we snap our fingers at you and at those you represent.
We ask, in the public interest; I go even further: we ask you, for the sake of patriotism, to appoint as returning officers the officials mentioned in the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Shelburne and (Queen's, men who enjoy the confidence of a considerable portion of our population; if they are not willing to serve; if, in any riding, none of those mentioned in the list are available, then a,ppoint somebody eke.
The argument of any friends from the West when they say: We have none of these officers in the West, is entirely irrelevant. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) even took occasion to state that certain public officials did not enjoy his confidence.
I might say that in English. I am stating that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) just now stated that certain officers appointed by this Government as customs officers were not proper men to be appointed, and at the same time to support his argument, he said-
I think the hon. member is misinterpreting the statement I made. I made no reference whatever to any officers that this Government had appointed.
I understood my hon. friend to say that certain customs officers were not acceptable to him, nor to the community. Is that right?
The inference I tried to draw was that no customs officer is satisfactory to me as a returning officer.

Or satisfactory to me.
Therefore, my hon. friend wants to support his argument that the Government can appoint as returning officers persons sat.io. factory to him, by saying that in appointments that have been previously made they have not appointed men who were satisfactory to him.
Now, I shall go on with my argument. I say that one of the most important tasks which confronts us to-day in this country
is that of building anew the confidence of the people in parliamentary government and J maintain that the appointment of the officials mentioned in the amendment of my hon. friend (iMr. Fielding) will go along way, in the older provinces, towards restoring that confidence.
The hon. members from the West tell us the Act is for the whole country. Exactly: the Act k concerned with Canada as a whole and not with the West exclusively. If the West be dissatisfied the latter part of this section offers the means for redress.
I appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who is better acquainted than any one eke with the respectability of our sheriffs, our registrars, and our prothonotaries-incidentally, I would request that the word "prothonot-ary" be added to the motion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, if there be no objection. I say that, in the past, up to 1917, as the hon. Minister of Justice is well aware, these officials acted as returning officers and were found satisfactory.
The argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia is this-I use hie own words -iWe have tried out this system and we know its worth.
Yes, we have tried this system, but under different conditions: we put it to the test, as I said before, when the people still had faith in parliamentary government, when they still believed in the men who were at the head of affairs in this country. The system was abandoned in 1917. In 1917, we set up the system that we want to impose on certain provinces that never used it before.
As pointed out by one of the hon. members who spoke before me, the voters' lists, in the different provinces, were drawn up by the municipalities, their revision was left to revisers appointed jointly by the municipalities and the Provincial Governments and once revised, they were accepted as final. Thereafter no one whose name did not appear on the list was entitled to cast a ballot, no matter what he did; even if he swore on oath that he was a duly qualified voter, it availed him nothing. When an election took place the returning officer appointed was a public official; his hearth and his family were in that very locality; he was known to every one; he had the honour of his family td safeguard; he was entrusted with a mission which did not end with the execution of the writ of election.

Therein lies the danger of appointing a man who is not a public official: once the election is over his responsibility ceases- I am not insinuating, mark you, that there are no honest men to be found outside those mentioned in the amendment submitted by my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's.
Spokesmen for the other side have tried to throw dust in our eyes; the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) tried to worry us by asking: "Would you accept a workingman?'' Of course we would accept a workingman. You will find workingmen amongst the postmaster and amongst the town clerks. 1 admit, however, that there are no labouring men to be found occupying positions which require legal qualifications. We must not forget, Mr. Chairman, that these men are quasi judicial officers. The moment a returning officer is appointed there is no appealing from his decision until after the election and then we can only have recourse against the individual who benefited or suffered through the returning officer's actions. These can be corrected solely by judgment rendered in court. Hence I maintain that since the returning officer is a' quasi judicial officer the greatest care must be exercised in selecting these men. What objection can the Minister of Militia have to appointing a registrar, where possible, in those provinces which are accustomed to that way of doing things. If he did that he would help to bring back public confidence and to persuade the people that parliamentary government is not farce, as a great many are inclined to believe nowadays, because we representatives of the people have been ignored right along.
Certain hon. gentlemen on the other side have sought to show that we wished to restrict the appointment of returning officers to the officials mentioned in the amendment submitted by the hony member for Shelburne and Queen's. That is absolutely false. If the man does not care to accept the appointment, if none of these officials be available; should you not have at hand any town clerk, nor any man whom you think qualified, then let the Governor General in Council appoint a man. But what we want, and it is only fair-I have so far heard nothing against the fairness of this proposal-is that where we have been accustomed to these officials, where they have already served as returning officers, and are there, ready to act in that capacity again; we ask the Government, I repeat, not to overlook these public servants when the time comes for appointing a returning offi-TMr. Bureau.] .
cer. The public interest demands that the appointments be made in that way.
I had nothing to complain about in 1917 since I was returned by acclamation; however, 1 feel quite sure that the gentleman appointed as returning officer in 1917-an eminently respectable gentleman; I have nothing to say against him-did not enjoy the confidence of the community to as great a decree as did the prothonotary of the Superior Court of the Three Rivers district who was chosen for the post in 1911.
The Government seems to look upon the appointment of a returning officer as if it were mere routine; as though the conduct of a returning officer were not of much account. This is a serious mistake.
I submit that we have established our case. We ask the House to accept the the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, in the public interest; we ask it for the sake of public confidence in the efficiency of parliamentary government, which we must restore.
The hon. Minister of Militia says he has not yet heard a single argument in favour of the amendment. If the public interest, if the restoring of public confidence in representative government are not sound arguments, then I must bow to the minister. At the same time if the public interest is not given precedence over all else, then I am forced to conclude that there are, behind this Bill, certain motives that will bear watching.
On the other hand I maintain that the Minister of Militia should give me a reason for refusing to accept this amendment. He says: We have tried the old law and found it satisfactory. I make this distinction, and I want to be clearly understood, that prior to 1917 conditions were not the same; the people did not think as they think today; they did not consider Parliament and the Government in the same light as they consider them to-day; there was none of the agitation which is>
everywhere prevalent to-day; there was none of the spirit of discontent which we have to-day. This discontent is levelled at Parliament and its institutions, and this is a natural consequence of the actions of a Government which has sought to administer the affairs of State by Order in Council, without consulting the representative of the people.
Under the circumstances I say that the burden of proof should not be on us, should not be on the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's; it is the Minister of Militia who should show cause for refusing to accept this amendment when we have made

it clear to him that in the name of public interest, in the name of patriotism the amendment should be accepted.
The Government on bringing down the Bill told us that the measure was intended to give fair treatment to all.
Sir, we do not deny the right of the Governor in Council, when he sees fit, to appoint as returning officer some one other than a post-master, a customs official, a pro-thonotary or a registrar; what we say is this: When you "can, and when public sentiment demands it, why mot, chose your returning officers from among these officials who are available for the work and well prepared for it? I repeat that the duties of a returning officer are of a high order of importance; and it is not any Tom, Dick or Harry who can measure up to them.
For these reasons, and in the public interest, as I have already said, I shall support to the utmost the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's.

One would scarcely expect, at this stage of the debate, to contribute any new thought to the arguments that have already been presented in reference to the clause under discussion. I am not able to convince myself that the Opposition really think they have submitted any strong arguments in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member (Mr. Fielding). The arguments that have been made remind me of the small country storekeeper who when his rival across the street was drawing the bulk of the trade to his store put in his window the sign " Do not go across there to be buncoed. Come in here." My hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) earnestly appeals to this Government to refrain from creating any machinery which may result in returning them to power, and I can imagine him saying, sotto voce, " Swing it over to this side."
I have not yet heard any answer to the arguments made yesterday by my hon. friend (Mr. Best) to the effect that the amendment discriminated against certain classes of the community who are entitled to consideration. I represent a rural constituency and I have been interested in elections for many years, and I know that in my district the practice has invariably been to' choose a reliable farmer as returning officer, and they have given unqualified satisfaction. In an experience of thirty years I cannot recall a single act done by any returning officer that has been brought into question in the slightest degree. I am 102
opposed to this amendment because it would prevent consideration being given to the farmers and also to labour, who are entitled to consideration. I cannot believe that we should get better officials by confining ourselves to the classes mentioned in the amendment, or that we will be any more likely to get away from partisanship.
I shall support the clause as submitted by the minister because I believe it is fair, and it allows of a wider selection in the appointment of officials. I believe that this election law can be administered without any dishonesty on the part of the men selected by the Government.

I object to clause 22 because it is partisan. The candidate supporting the Government has the naming of the returning officer; the returning officer has the naming of his deputies, and of the registrars and poll clerks. From the very beginning the thing is unfair. I know it to be unfair because I have had experience on two occasions myself. Under the party system I had the naming of the returning officer. What did I do? I tried to pick a man at least as partisan as myself, and I succeeded. Now that is an unfair advantage, there is no question about it. This officer has power to influence not only his officials but very many voters. He decides where the polling station shall be located and whose house shall be rented. It is patronage of the most vicious kind, and I must plead guilty of this offence twice. We were told when the Union Government was appealing to the country that patronage would be abolished, that a new political era had arrived, that everything would be good from now on. Now is the time for hon. gentlemen opposite to make good their word. The sins they have to answer for are many, but they might as well leave power with the credit of having been fair once. They can be fair by accepting the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding). There is no question that they are going to leave power, because throughout the length and breadth of the land the electors have learnt to hate them, to detest and despise and desert them. A certain number of the Government's followers deserted them last night because they knew that the day of reckoning was near at hand when they would have to appeal to the men who voted for them the last time. And I can tell some hon. gentlemen this also, that there are in this House many men whom we and the country know to be "compromise" candidates. They are com-



promised candidates for the reason that when the Union party was formed, if a constituency was allotted to a Conservative candidate, the Union Liberals would not accept a Conservative whom they considered to be a strong man. They demanded that a weak man should be chosen because they contended that the Union Government was only a temporary expedient, and they did not desire to place in power any man whom they would find it difficult to defeat when the union was dissolved and party politics were resumed. I therefore say that there are hon. gentlemen who were compromise candidates, and although they may vote for this measure it. will not help them in any way, for they will not be elected again. They will not be elected for the simple reason that the majority of them will not be nominated again. I say to this Government that they ought, as honourable men, to be fair in the appointing of returning officers. But even if it were in the power of this Government to make every man in Canada a returning officer the Government would be defeated just the same. Ilf this Bill goes through I shall of course be bound to accept it and I shall do the best I can to have it observed. But it is most unfair, and this Government, which we were told was formed for the sole purpose of saving the British Empire, Canada and humanity, ought to realize the necessity for justice and fair play in this matter. They have nothing to lose but everything to gain by being perfectly honest and fair. I recall, in considering the unfairness of this Act, a story which was told of General Sam Steele many years ago in Western Canada. We believe that no braver man than General Steele ever lived, and on one occasion, when he was in very close quarters and pitted against great odds, he made an address in which he said that it did not make so much difference how long a man lived, in view of the immortality of the soul and the eternity of time, but that it did make a great difference what name he left behind him. This Government, rightly or wrongly, is charged by the people with having been derelict and unfair in the administration of the affairs of the country, and that they will be defeated there is no possible question. In view of this probability-nay, this certainty-does it not behoove them to leave behind them a name which will at all events partly redeem their errors? That they will not be re-elected they know perfectly well.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.
Every one says so.
Question.
Hear, hear.

The people generally, including gentlemen opposite themselves, know this to be true. Now, as regards the different offices that have been named, I am prepared to say that if I am a candidate again in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, I am willing, and indeed I would prefer, to accept such men as municipal clerks or Secretary-treasurers in any municipality in Provencher, and some are Conservative and some are Liberal. I am quite satisfied to have any one of these men nominated, and if I had the naming of them I would select them whether they were Liberal or Conservative. There are no more Unionists there, so that any man appointed would have to be a Conservative or a Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: What about a farmer?

Yes. Hon. gentlemen are pleading for the farmers, and it has been said that the farmers will not get in on this. The hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best) last night was worried about the farmers, but let me say to that hon. gentleman and others on the opposite side that they would do well to look out for the farmers, for there is no doubt whatever that the farmers, to use the common expression, will fix them all right. In the county of Dufferin, where, in the old days, a Liberal candidate was lucky to save his deposit, and where the present member (Mr. Best) was elected in 1917 by 2,500 or mdre, in the last provincial election, a U.F.O. candidate carried the seat by a majority of about 600. I am not worrying about the farmers, and II am quite ready to take my chance with the farmer and the Unionist, and I shall be glad to meet on common ground with any Tory.
Mr. Chairman, I move that we call it six o'clock.
No. Go on.

Well, I have no objection
to continuing this very pleasant debate. I was rather aipused during the course of remarks to which I have listened from hon. members opposite to hear their pleas on behalf of the farmer, the labouring man, and the returned soldier. I quite agree that the farmer, the labourer, and the returned

soldier should be given some opportunity of exercising their peculiar qualifications in the position of returning officer. But to my mind the offipe of returning officer, and some other positions mentioned, should not be held hy men who do not possess a certain legal knowledge. These men need not necessarily be barristers or solicitors, but in a large number of cases their functions are necessarily judicial, or at least, as my hon. friend - from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) suggests, quasi-judicial, and in some instances they exercise functions that are almost purely legal. Without having had a certain legal training he would have innumerable difficulties in administering the duties of his position fairly and equitably. In reference to the returned soldier, from my knowledge of that gentleman, it is hardly likely that he will be appointed as a returning officer because, knowing the extreme partiality which has been manifested by the Government to the returned soldier in giving him a position so that he may be able to earn sufficient money to re-establish himself, I am quite sure that he will not be satisfied with an appointment that will give him $2 or $3 a day for five or six days. A returned soldier who will be satisfied with such a position, or who will not be sufficiently reestablished that he will want that position, will not be the class of man we want as a returning officer. I will go further for the benefit of those who wish to have the returned soldier. It seems to me that this law has already been sufficiently surrounded by militarism without introducing the returned soldier into the question. We had in the past' the Minister of Militia and they had a legal adviser to the Militia Department. We have been fighting for years against militarism, I understand that the adviser is the legal adviser to the Militia Department and I understand that he has had considerable experience in reference to military votes. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) who sits behind him, and doubtless whispers words of wisdom into his ear, is also a soldier and perhaps will know how to manage the military vote. I protest, as one who has invariably protested, against militarizing the Franchise Act. I had experience of it in 1917 and I sincerely hope with the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Molloy) that this Government, bad as it is, will when it departs this life, have obtained and ah tained that position that those who will came after will be able to , say de mortuis nil nisi bonum.
Progress reported.
