May I ask the hon. minister to make a statement to the House in respect to the icebreakers? This year we have had the "Lady Grey" on the St. Lawrence route, but although the winter was very severe I understand the "Montcalm" was engaged elsewhere. Is it the intention of the Government to improve the service of icebreakers on the St. Lawrence route between Quebec and Montreal so as to keep the channel clear and prevent floods in the spring?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In addition to the icebreakers that the Government have had in service for some years on the St. Lawrence, we purpose placing another icebreaker in commission, for which an item will be found a little further on in my Estimates for new icebreakers to cost approximately $2,000,000, and I hope the committee will approve of that item. iSo far as this particular vote is concerned, I may say that it is similar to that of last year's, being required to cover the operating and maintenance expense of twenty-four Government ships employed maintaining the light buoys and fog alarms in order and attending to construction work on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and on the lakes and rivers.

The "Montcalm" and
"(Lady 'Grey" are included in those twenty-four ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Does the maintenance include the wages of the seamen?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, the whole expense.

How much was expended on this item last year?
Mr. BALLAiNTYNE:	To March 1, 1920,

_ Mr. J. E. SINCLAIR:	Does this item
include the tugs and boats used by the Marine Department around the harbours?
Mr. BALLANTYNE,:	It includes everything that is operated by the Marine Department, with the exception of the small 
tugs that are used in connection with dredging the St. Lawrence ship channel.

In regard to the
salaries of the engineers on the small tugs on the eastern coast-and, I refer especially to the "IBrant"-I understand that representations have been made to the department that their scale of pay is not in accordance with the scale of the National Association of Marine Engineers. Has the department under consideration adjusting those wages; and, if so, what change does the hon. minister purpose making in the way of an advance?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Under the proposed increase will the engineers be entitled to the bonus that is being paid to civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My department has to pay the prevailing rate of wages, and therefore it is not deemed advisable to give these men any bonus. Besides, they are in an entirely different position from the men employed in other branches of the Civil Service.

In making the
proposed increase does the minister intend to accept the scale of pay adopted for Eastern Canada by the Association of Marine Engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For the moment I have not before me the schedule of wages my hon. friend refers to. I cannot make any definite promise in that regard beyond what I said a moment ago. I will be very glad to do whatever is fair and right, but I am not prepared to say that we will give exactly the same wages down on the Atlantic coast as out on the Pacific coast. For the moment 1 do not know the difference that my hon. friend refers to.
In what way do you distinguish between the Atlantic and the Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no uniform scale of wages; it depends a good deal upon the ship and the service that she is

engaged in. The cost of living is higher on the Pacific coast than it is on the Atlantic.

The scale of
wages that has been adopted by the marine engineers for Eastern Canada is the same as the scale applying to those engaged in similar employment in private enterprise. Under the Association of Marine Engineers, chief engineers in private employment and working on such a steamer as I have mentioned dre entitled to a wage of $125 a month, and second engineers to $100 a month. When they are laid off during the winter months a bonus of twenty per cent over these wages is allowed. I think that the department has been a little close with the officers on the boat that I have mentioned in not giving them an increase when they are laid off during the winter months, as they have been for the past two years. Have these circumstances been brought to the minister's attention, and if so does he intend to place his engineers on the same level as those engaged in private employment as respects the granting of an increase when they are laid off during winter months?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The wages of the
engineers range from $80 to $175 a month. The larger the ship, the more the engineer is paid. The salaries of the chief engineers are as follows: "Aberdeen, $120 a month; "Aranmore," $130; "Argenteuil," $85; "Bellechasse," $115; "Brant"-the boat my hon. friend is referring to-$100; "Champlain," $100. And so on. They go down as low as $80.	.
According to the horse-power?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. I't has been the custom of my department to allow the men to receive their wages during the winter months.

I understand that in making the increase that the minister has not decided to adopt the scale of pay set forth toy the Association of Marine Engineers, and that he is going to discontinue the bonus. That may make the condition worse than it is. I ask the minister to take into consideration the cost of living and the general conditions applicable to the service of these men. When the steamer "Brant" lays off for the winter, what does it cost to keep her at the dock? How much is paid out for repairs while the ship is laid off during the winter that might be made
by these officers if they were kept at their posts?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have under consideration the matter of increases in salaries of all officers and men on the Government ships. When that increase is finally determined upon, the wage will equal that which was paid last year plus the bonus, so that the men will be just as well off in the present fiscal year as they were last year. When the department pays the same wage as the men would get anywhere else on similar ships, I think that they are being very well treated. We keep the ships in service as long as the weather permits and their services are required.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Is the minister in a position to make a statement regarding the icebreaker that was sent to Russia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot give any more information than I gave last year. The icebreaker "J. D. Hazen," which cost approximately $1,000,000, was sold to the Russian Government. Officers of my department have made every effort during the last two months to get trace of her, but have been unable to do so. Later on in my Estimates I am going to ask the committee to vote $2,000,000 for a similar icebreaker.
I hope it will not be for Russia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

It seems to me that it is unnecessary and unfair to pay a scale of wages on the Atlantic coast different from that which is paid on the Pacific coast. This old idea that it cost more to live in one part of Canada than it does in another is more or less a myth. The Government have gone into the operation of steamships, and it is about time the department realized that the eastern part of the Dominion is quite as important as, if not more important than, the western part. The services of a captain or engineer or any of the officers and men who are manning the boats on the Pacific coast are worth no more than the services of men doing similar work in boats on the Atlantic coast. The time has suTely arrived when there should be a uniform scale of wages on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am much in sympathy with the remarks of the hon. member. But it is a well recognized fact that, generally speaking, wages are much higher on the Pacific coast than they are in Eastern Canada, and we are forced to pay a

higher scale of wages out there. I will make every possible effort to bring the scale of wages of those employed on Government steamers in Eastern Canada, if not up to what is paid on the Pacific coast, at least as close as it is possible.

I would like my hon. friend to go further than that. There is no good reason why the wages should not be on a uniform basis. The work is just as hazardous in one place as in the oilier; if anything, it is more hazardous on the Atlantic coast. The work on the Atlantic is just as important and the men are just as well qualified for the positions as are the men who work in the West. I urge very strongly that the minister say here and now that those men who are doing splendid service on the Atlantic coast shall receive the same wages as those who are doing similar work on the Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In these days of
rigid economy when I have been held down so closely, and rightly so, by my colleague the Minister of Finance, I do not want to make any rash promises or any promises that I would not be able to fulfil. I will do the very best I can with the appropriation at my disposal, but beyond that, I cannot make any definite statement.

I am very glad to assist my hon. friend in the matter of economy. * If he cannot bring the wages of those operating on the Atlantic coast up to the scale of wages of those operating on the Pacific coast, he could, as a matter of economy, bring down the wages of those operating on the Pacific coast to the scale of wages of those operating on the Atlantic coast.
I wish to impress upon the minister as strongly as I possibly can the necessity of paying. uniform wages; and if my hon. friend wants to preach economy, I would suggest that if the men on the Atlantic coast are sufficiently paid with the wages they are now getting, he should bring down the wages of those operating on the Pacific coast to the same level. Then, he would have a uniform wage and would be saving money to the country at the same time.
How many icebreakers have we in Canada? What are their names, tonnage and ages? The minister might, perhaps, give us some idea where they are placed and what icebreaking work they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government
have three icebreakers, the Lady Grey, the Montcalm, and the Stanley. The Montcalm, with the exception of the past win-
ter, was engaged with the Lady Grey in keeping the ice broken at Cap Rouge, so as to avoid, as far as humanly possible, the possibility of floods in the spring. These icebreakers also, as soon as they can, keep working up the channel between Quebec and Montreal. The Lady Grey at the present time has been able to reach Montreal after some six weeks breaking ice from Quebec upwards. The Montcalm, owing to the wreck of the Aranmore, had to go down to the relief of the lighthouse keepers. She tried to reach the Magdalen islands and eventually did so after having been hemmed in the ice for a month. The other icebreaker, the Stanley, breaks ice on the Atlantic coast.

It is, I suppose, a very nice idea to keep the icebreaker at Cap Rouge where the minister has reason to dread these floods, but I am not so clear that it is quite good governmental policy to be breaking ice to avoid floods. There surely ought to be some means whereby the formation of that dangerous ice could be prevented. I notice that, in large rivers in the United States, roof-like structures are put into the rivers to prevent the formation of ice, and the ice runs up on them and breaks. Possibly such structures could not be placed at those points about which the minister speaks; but in the case I have spoken of, the formation of heavy ice or jams is prevented. There are in Canada places where icebreakers would be of great commercial assistance. The minister is, and has reason to be, proud of his plate mill at Sydney, and the country, I think, will be proud of the great development following the construction of that mill and other extensions in the industry in that part of the country. We are sometimes bothered with ice in Sydney harbour, and if the minister could give us the services of those icebreakers during a couple [DOT] of months in the year to keep the ice broken in Sydney harbour, he would be rendering great service to that industry which has done so much good at that place. It must be quite evident to the minister that those plates can be more cheaply carried from Sydney to other parts of the world by water than in any other way, and, therefore, it is of the greatest importance that navigation should be continuous. Icebreaking would be required during only about two months in the year, sometimes not even a month; in a mild winter, the icebreaker would not be required at all. But in a winter like the last, when the frost was

very severe, there were several weeks when steamers could not get in or out oi Sydney harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
is quite right in recommending that an icebreaker be employed when she is required at the port of Sydney. The Stanley has generally been allocated for that purpose, but unfortunately during the past winter she was disabled. The repairs are about completed now, and next winter she will be at Sydney harbour whenever the services of an icebreaker are required there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister
will recall that during last winter I had some correspondence with him regarding the condition of the people on the Magdalen islands. Has he taken into account the possibility of a similar situation arising .another winter, and is he making, in his Estimates, any provision to meet a situation of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I hope that before
the season closes for the present year, a sufficient quantity of provisions will be sent to the Magdalen islands. The reason that they were short of provisions during the past winter was because the steamer that was on that route became disabled, and it was very late in the season when the people living on the Magdalen islands called upon the Government to try to send provisions there. Owing to the lateness of the season, the ship got stuck in the ice and it was necessary to send the icebreaker Montcalm there. I hope nothing will happen to the steamer on this route during the coming season, and that the island will have all the provisions necessary before the extreme weather comes on. If not, my department will send whatever available icebreaker we may have to the assistance of such ships in distress.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it possible in any way to get the people of the islands to appreciate the necessity of importing the necessaries of life during the open season? It seems to me that a good deal of the difficulty that arose came from the fact the minister mentioned, namely, that supplies had not been brought in at the right time. Could the Government do anything in the way of notifying some of the merchants on the island as to the necessity of early importations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The leader of the
Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is quite right. The importance of the Magdalen Island people stocking up with the necessary
provisions will be brought to their attention by the Acting Prime Minister who is also Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). The matter comes under his department and I shall have pleasure in bringing the matter to his attention. I might say that in former years sudh trouble has not been experienced but the circumstances have been unusual of late, owing to the war and the extreme shortage of tonnage, and the unfortunate accident to the steamer that was on the route.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I notice that the minister intends to ask for an appropriation for the construction of an icebreaker steamer to be used on the River St. Lawrence. At the present time there is a car ferry that plies between the mainland and Prince Edward Island from Cape Tormen-tine to Port Borden. As the minister is aware, that ferry is used for carrying cars and is also often used to help out in different places where emergencies arise. It has been suggested that when the department undertakes the construction of an icebreaker, it might be possible to have it so constructed that it will serve the purposes of a car ferry in the summer season and of an icebreaker in the winter season. I am told that leading marine experts believe that this is quite feasible. As an, expenditure of $2,000,000 is to be made on an icebreaker, if it could be so constructed as to serve also the purposes of a car ferry, it would perhaps postpone the time when a second car ferry would be established between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I think there is a necessity at the present time for a second car ferry, but we realize that these are days when economy is also needed. This two-fold object might be attained if the minister, in arranging for the construction of this icebreaker could have it made to serve tfhe double purpose I have mentioned. If anything should happen to the present ferry the people of the Island would be cut off completely in their trade accommodation. They have become accustomed to using the ferry, and any misfortune to it would be seriously felt. I would ask the minister whether he has considered having the icebreaker made to serve this double purpose, and if he has not, would he find out before undertaking construction if such a plan is feasible?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The department has not yet called for tenders. I was awaiting the approval of this committee before doing

so. I am not enough of a technical man myself to know whether it is feasible to have an icebreaker as large and as powerful as the one we have in contemplation made to serve also the purposes of a car ferry, but the suggestion is well worthy of consideration, and I shall be very glad to talk it over with the shipbuilders. The icebreaker that we have in mind will be so powerful that she will be able to cut her way through ice at any time of the year wherever she may he, and on account of her strength it may not be possible to have her so constructed as to serve this other purpose. If the shipbuilders, however, think it is at all feasible.I shall be glad to do it.

I should like to emphasise what the leader of the Opposition has said. As the minister knows, the boat that is now in operation as a car ferry between Prince Edward Island and the mainland is the most powerful icebreaker we now have on the Atlantic coast, and it does good work. Those who know ice conditions in the East are of opinion that it is quite feasible to have a boat built to serve both as car ferry and icebreaker. That would give us a boat that would be able both to relieve the car ferry and take care of ice conditions. The minister will remember that during the past season when a boat of the merchant marine got fast in the ice of the St. Lawrence, strong representations were made to the Railway Department to have the car ferry taken off the route. That would have been a calamity to the province of Prince Edward Island, because she was doing good work, and was the only means of communication we had with the mainland. She was continuously employed night and day to keep open communication. At the present time, when we are forced to practise economy to such a rigid extent, I think it would be wise to consider having this icebreaker so constructed that it will serve both purposes, and I trust that the minister will take the matter up with the Railway Department and ascertain whether or not it is feasible.

How many icebreakers were sold to Russia by this Government, and at what price?
Mr. BALLANTYNE.: The previous government sold three Canadian icebreakers to the Russian Government. The "J. D. Hazen,' the powerful one that I referred to a moment ago, costing at that time $1,000,000, and of which we hope to construct a 
duplicate; the "Earl Grey" and "The Minto."
In what y-ear were they sold?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In 1916. I understand the Government of that day got cost price for the icebreakers.
Were they paid for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We are anxious to assist the minister in getting his Estimates through, but he will observe that we have Tather a thin House to-night, and I know that one or two members are particularly interested in certain of these items. If we allow these items to pass, but reserve one or two, I presume it can be understood that in subsequent discussions we shall be free to refer to any item that has passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite so.
In contracting for a new and possibly an improved "J. D. Hazen," the icebreaker the minister has spoken of, does he intend to go back to the somewhat antiquated idea of calling for tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Tenders, cf course, will be called for now that the emergency no longer exists.

I might say for the information of the minister that an emergency does exist in the need for icebreakers for winter navigation of the St. Lawrence-a far greater emergency than existed at the time he gave the contracts for the merchant marine. However, I did not rise to speak of the new icebreaker, but more with reference to repairs to the old icebreakers. May I ask where these repairs were made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At the Davie Shipbuilding Company, Quebec.
All of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, so far as I know.

Is the Government not the proprietor of a drydock at Levis that might very well have been used for repairing these ships? If the Government is the proprietor and manager of this drydock, why don't they send their own ships to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The drydock at
Lauzon comes under the Department of Public Works and is leased to the Davie Shipbuilding Company. The Government of course do own the dock but have no ship repairing plant there.
What is the cost of repairs to icebreakers for the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have not that information available but I shall try to get
it.

Will the minister give us the cost of repairs to 'any other government boats? I ask this question because it might be possible for the Government to install a ship-repairing plant in this dry dock [DOT]with a view to economizing a little. I am not sure that very great economy would be effected, but if the bill for repairs is exorbitant it is quite likely that by doing their own repairs the Government could save money. They might nationalize a system of repairs, seeing that they have nationalized other things that should have been left alone. If it can be shown that the Gov-ment could save money by carrying on their own repairs I think they should take this matter into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The experience of
my department has been quite the opposite. There is only a limited amount of repairs to be done, and it has been found to be in the public interest to give the work out. I do not desire to deviate from the Estimates now under consideration except to say that I now have under consideration the closing up of some naval shops, and the Marine Department's experience at Sorel shows quite clearly that it is in the public interest to have the work done outside, because we have not a sufficient amount of work to keep a repair shop fairly busy throughout the year. The value of repairs for the twenty-four ships we have in commission, and for which this vote is asked, varies year by year, but generally it runs up to about $300,000 a year, and I do not think it would be advisable to establish a ship-repairing plant and install the necessary machinery to do the work when, although we occasionally have considerable work to do, there is generally little work on hand. In managing a ship-repairing plant of this character we would have to keep skilled men on whether or not we had work to keep them busy all the time. It is, therefore, an economy to send out the work.

I placed a question on the Order Paper some days ago with reference to the uniforms worn'by the men on the Lady Grey, which I understand is an icebreaker. The information I received was that the contract for these uniforms was given to a concern known as the Christie Clothing Company of Montreal, after satisfactory prices had been agreed upon with the company. No tender appears to have been called for. The " antiquated method " referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) a few moments ago was certainly not put into force in this instance. Was there an "emergency"? I understand that it is now quite the thing for employees of the Government to wear their old clothes, and perhaps the crew of the Lady Grey might have worn their old clothes for a few days more, in the " emergency," so that tenders might have been called for.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) drew my attention a year ago to the rather faded appearance of the uniforms which the officers and men on government steamers were wearing, and referred particularly to the Lake Champlain and the Lady Grey.
I quite agreed with the hon. member at that time, and accordingjy gave instructions that uniforms should be ordered. Public tenders were called for, but when a few additional uniforms were needed, the purchasing agent placed them with the firm to which he had previously given the contract. I do not want my hon. friend to think that uniforms on a large scale are ordered without tenders being called for.

Apparently they were in
this case, the old ones having offended the artistic eye of the member for Charlevoix-Montmorency. Can the minister say what was the total amount of this contract?
Mr. BALLANTY'NE: I have not that information here.

The amount must have
been fairly large because, for chief officer's uniforms, the price was $35, officers' suits, $32, and so on. The fact that the Christie .Clothing Company might have been able to supply uniforms at more satisfactory rates than other firms on a previous occasion should not justify the purchasing agent in going only to them when more goods are required. It would seem unreasonable, in the light of their experience, that the other firms that were unsuccessful in bidding for uniforms on another boat would have quoted more satisfactory prices had tenders been called for in the case of the Lady Grey. It is not a sufficient justification for this lack of economy to say that because a satisfactory tender had been received once from the Christie Clothing Company we ought to continue obtaining clothing from them alone for another year or as long as the minister thinks fit. Was this contract given through the War Purchasing Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be glad to get the information the hon. gentleman asks for. It is difficult to anticipate all these questions, but the question the hon. member asks is certainly a reasonable one, and when I am on my Estimates again I shall see that the information he asks for is available. I am under the impression that the .quantity was not large, but, as I say, I .shall have more definite information on another occasion. A sufficient quantity of uniforms has been ordered to supply all the officers and men on the Government ships.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Some twenty years ago a resolution was passed unanimously in this House with regard to Government clothing contracts, and according to the termjs of that resolution all contracts for clothing for Government officials were to be awarded only after tenders had been called for, and after the Department of .Labour had been given an opportunity of fixing a minimum wage for the workers, and of providing the proper inspection of premises in which the work was to be carried on. It had been found in connection with clothing for the Militia Department that contracts had been awarded to certain parties who sub-let the contracts, which were sublet again, with the result that the work wajs finally carried out in sweat shops, the workers receiving very few cents per hour, and the contractors making a profit of a .hundred, or a hundred and fifty, or two hundred per cent. That condition was brought out in a report which was submitted to Parliament and this resolution was pasjsed unanimously by Parliament at the time. Probably the minister may not have seen the resolution, but it is still an order to the different departments, and I hope that in small things as well as great, in the expenditures for clothing as well as in the millions on these ships, he will watch the resolutions of the House that have been passed for the protection of labour and the promotion of economy.

I wish to draw the minister's attention to a more or less satisfactory answer which was given to a question that I placed on the Order Paper. In answer to a question asked on April 7 it was stated by the minister that "uniforms for the 'Lady Grey' were ordered after satisfactory prices were arranged for a suitable quality of material." I had asked what these satisfactory prices were and where the material was purchased, and the answer was: "From the Christie Clothing Company, Montreal." 
What I want to know is why the minister did not give us the reason for not calling for tenders for uniforms for the officers and crew of the "Lady Grey" other than saying "they were ordered after satisfactory prices were arranged for a suitable quality of material." The fact that certain material was to be obtained at Christie's is surely not a sufficient reason for telling us that they alone should be awarded the contract. Surely other .firms in Montreal or Quebec could have .purchased from whatever quarter of the globe this material comes, and could have obtained an equally satisfactory quality. It is not sufficient for the minister to say, "We bought from that firm because they had the material," and leave us to understand that only the Christie Company could obtain this quality. Are we to understand that the "Lady Grey" required a quality of material that only the Christie Company could supply, whereas the other government boats could be supplied by other firms? Is there anything special about the uniforms for the officers and crew of the "Lady Grey" that they should be made of a particular material?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would be surprised if there was only one firm that could supply the necessary quality. I confess that from the answer it looks as if that were so, but my deputy has just gone to the telephone to get more particulars than what I have at the moment, and I would ask my hon. friend to allow the question to stand and I will give him the information later on.
Is the minister able to tell us how much the Davie Shipbuiding Company is paying for the use of the dry dock?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As dry docks come under the Department of Public Works, I am sorry I am not able to give the information.
What was paid to the Davie Shipbuilding Company for repairs to government boats last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not in a position to give that information for each steamer; I can only give the lump sum.
I would like to know the lump sum paid to the Davie Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Estimates for
general repairs run about $300,000 per year, but just how much was actually paid to the

Davie Shipbuilding Company 9 p.m. for the past fiscal year I will have to find out and let the hon. gentleman know.

Was the icebreaker
"Stanley" repaired by the Davie Shipbuilding Company or at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At Halifax.

Was the "Montcalm" repaired at Halifax or at the Davie dry dock?
I understand that steamer also was very badly damaged last winter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The "Stanley" was damaged on the Atlantic coast and it was impossible to get her up to Levis owing to the lateness of the season. We cannot tell what the repairs will be until a survey has been made and a report rendered. Any further repairs that may be required by this steamer will be made by the Davie Shipbuilding Company.
What about the "Montcalm?"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The "Montcalm," as a general rule, is repaired by the Davie Shipbuilding Company, but this year she had to go down to the assistance of the lighthouse keepers and later came up to relieve the Government steamer "Spinner." Then she went to the Magdalen Islands and necessarily had to go to Halifax to have repairs made as she was unable to come up to Quebec owing to the ice. As a rule she is not on the Atlantic coast during winter, but is around Quebec.
What is the name of the firm in charge of repairs at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Halifax Shipyards,' Limited.

How many icebreakers
were in commission and fit for service during the late autumn and winter of 1919 in the St. Lawrence river?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The "Lady Grey" and the "Montcalm."

Could the minister tell me why the "Lady Grey" and "Montcalm" were unable to proceed to Belle Isle and were unable to escort the Canadian Government boats which left Quebec late in the season to such an extent that these boats had a very hard time, and in fact one was wrecked owing to the fact that no icebreaker was there to render assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The "Montcalm"
was not there. The "Lady Grey," owing to being only able to carry a certain amount of coal, to the severity of the weatheT, to the mist caused by the extreme cold, and to the unusual thickness of the ice, was unable to go to the relief of the Government steamer "Spinner." That is one of the reasons why I am going to ask the committee to vote $2,000,000 for a much more powerful icebreaker than the "Lady Grey."

I understand the minister
to say that the "Montcalm" was available in the early winter. Where was she?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The "Montcalm"
was around Belle Isle trying to relieve the lighthouse keepers. She was sent down there because the "Aranmore," loaded with lighthouse supplies, was wrecked, and these lighthouse keepers were almost on the verge of starvation. We sent the "Montcalm" down there to relieve them, but she was unable to do so, and the Marine Department thereupon arranged with the Government of Newfoundland to send a relief ship. That accounts for the "Aranmore" being in that district instead of around Quebec.

At what period of the
year has it been the custom to supply the people at Belle Isle with provisions?
Mr, BALLANTYNE: Any time up to the close of navigation, but the supplies were despatched a little later than usual last vear owing to the department being short of ships, having sold the ships that I mentioned to the Russian Government, and other ships having been wrecked. It was just one of those 'unfortunate accidents that occur occasionally.
M.r. POWER: It seems to me that proper precautions might be taken to deliver supplies in the middle oi summer or at any rate when the department is sure navigation will be open. The officials of the department must know that in the late autumn these storms are apt to occur-they occur nearly every autumn. These deplorable' circumstances might have been avoided had proper precautions been taken in due time to supply the people at Belle Isle and the Magdalen Islands.
iMt. BALLANTYNE:	The "Aranmore"
was ordered in good time to take provisions to the lighthouse keepers, but an emergency call came from a steamer in distress, and we had to send the "Aranmore" to her rescue because quite a number of the crew were adrift in small boats.

The "Aranmore" no sooner performed that service than she got toother call to go to the rescue of a second steamer in distress.

lls the "Aranmore" a
complete loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, there is a very fair possibility of our being able to salvage her.

I do not know whether my question will be in order on this item, but I would like to get some information regarding the crew of the icebreaker "Montcalm," some of whom I understand, left their ship during the winter. According to the newspapers those men maintain that they were unable to return to their ship owing to the fact that the ice had in the meantime opened up, but I saw a report from the minister or from his department, if I remember rightly, that these men were deserters. I would like to know what is their status?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Their statujs is just exactly as my hon. friend states-deserters. The Montcalm was stuck in the ice in her endeavour to reach the Magdalen Islands, but there was really no danger sufficient to warrant sixteen men deserting her, more particularly when she was on the important service of carrying supplies to people on the verge of starvation. These men deserted tlieir ship and are now open to prosecution if the department desires to take action.
I am to understand, then, from the answer of the minister that thase men have not been prosecuted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have not been prosecuted.

I am not very familiar with marine law, but I do not think the minister should accuse these men of being deserters before they have had'an opportunity of defending themselves. I see the Minister of [DOT]Justi'ce (Mr. Doherty) coming in now. We heard him last night expatiating at great length oh the iniquity of condemning people who have not had a chance to defend themselves. Here we have sixteen brave mariners-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not very brave.

That, 1 am sure the minister will admit, is a. matter of appreciation. We have sixteen mariners, who, if I may believe the stories they have given to the newspapers, left the ship with, at any rate, the consent of their captain to go for a walk fMr. Ballantyne.]
on the ice, but when they endeavoured to return they found that a break in the ice prevented them. So they went to their homes, and apparently they acted in good faith, because they made no secret of it, and had to be helped homeward by some charitable souls. It seems to me that before using such a harsh word the minister ought to have made an investigation and ordered the prosecution of these men. Apparently nothing has been done. I would like to know where the minijster gets the information that leads him to call these men deserters, and whether he intends to pay them their wages.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
being a military man with a very fine record at the front, knows very well the definition of "deserter." When a soldier deserts from the front line no investigation is necessary.
1 Mr. POWER: A court-martial ijs necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Except a courtmartial. If a soldier deserts my hon. friend knows what the penalty is.

But even in the army a
man is never condemned unheard.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have a slight
knowledge of military matters myself, and I say that if a man deserted in the front- line he would be court-martialled and shot at dawn. Here was a ship on a mission of mercy to people almost on the verge of starvation, and the men were in no danger whatever. Apparently these sixteen men got tired of being stuck in the ice on board the Montcalm, deserted, and had no desire to return to their ship. I have no words strong enough to express my condemnation of such action. Seamen ajs a class generally perform their duty, but these men failed when they were most urgently needed. I am convinced that the department and the captain were justified in not paying these deserters their wages, and they must consider themselves lucky in escaping prosecution.

But the hon. minister has told uis that these men are deserters, although they have never been tried and convicted. I am sure he must have some information to justify his use of such a harsh term, and, being a fair-minded man, I hope he will give the committee the advantage of that information so that we may form our own judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, if the hon. member is of the opinion that my department should prosecute these men, I am

quite willing to do so; then they will have a fair trial before . a proper tribunal.

No, I am of the opinion that the department should prosecute them, hut I am of the opinion that the minister, before branding them as deserters, should have held some investigation; should have had what is equivalent to a military court martial; should at least have become acquainted with the facts; should have heard the excuse given by the men. Their excuse seems to be a fairly reasonable one. I do not know anything about it, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is it?

It is said that their ship was apparently stuck fast in the ice and that the captain consented to their going for a walk on the ice; that would be a legitimate thing for the captain to do, I suppose, especially in view of the fact that the men had been cooped up in the boat for several weeks. In those circumstances a walk on the ice would be a good thing for the crew. Well, they went out for the walk and when they attempted to return [DOT]they found that there was a break in the ice which prevented them from reaching the ship. Therefore they went ashore, and judging from the reports, they suffered almost incredible hardships in doing so. There seems to be a prima facie case in favour of their having a reasonable excuse for their so-called desertion. The minister might have made an investigation; might have looked into the matter before he branded these men as deserters. I quite agree that they should not be excused if they deliberately deserted the ship, but in any case they should be given a chance; they should be given a hearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The report of Captain Hearn does not in any way state that the men went out for a little exercise on the ice and were unable to return. Captain Hearn reports-and he is one of the best captains that we have-that these men did not go for a walk except with the intention of taking a long walk to reach the shore and not to return to the ship.
Have any protests been received from members of the crew? Have any demands been received from them regarding their pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Leaving aside the question of desertion, I understand, then, that the department is willing to accept the captain's statement so far as pay is concerned. The captain says that we do not owe these men any money; therefore we shall not pay them. Is that the case?
Mr. BALLANTYNE;: Does the hon. member want an investigation, which will prove rather serious for the men? I shall be very glad to see that an investigation is held.
If the men have demanded their pay I think they should be given an investigation. It would be more satisfactory for all concerned if that were done.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It will be done.

On this item I would like to direct attention to a matter in which my constituents are interested-not by way of complaint, because it is a matter in which the minister has been very considerate and courteous; but I want to speak now with a view of helping him to render even more efficient service in the future. In an ordinary winter the ports on the south shore of Nova Scotia are usually open. But there are times when as a result ot severe cold-we have lately had several winters of that kind-these ports are closed. For example, during the past winter the port of Shelburne, where large shipbuilding operations are carried on, was closed for a few days; and the port of Lookeport, the centre of large fishing operations, also was closed. A year ago I brought this matter to the minister's attention and he very kindly gave instructions to the fleet at Halifax to do the best they could to keep these harbours open, and I know that he did the same thing during the past winter. But the trouble is that he has not the necessary equipment; the small vessels which are available for the purpose are useful only when the ice is exceedingly thin-in fact, if the ice is formed at all these vessels are not suited to the purpose. Although these are times of economy, there are some things in which we cannot very well economize. 1 think it is important that the Department of Marine should have one or two vessels, not entirely for icebreaking, but of sufficient power to be used as icebreakers in the cases to which I refer. I suggest that my hon. friend see that he has available for future winters a vessel of somewhat better power than those which have been used in the past so ' that these ports may be kept open. The matter is important in a business way. The fishing business, for example, is developing very rapidly, and if a port which is made

the headquarters of a large fishing fleet is closed by ice for some days, it is a matter of more than local importance; it affects wide interests. The shipbuilding operations also at Shelburne should not be interfered with in this way. I repeat' that I am not complaining; on the contrary I wish to express appreciation of the efforts the minister has made in this direction. I hope that in the coming winter he will have a better equipment available in order that more efficient service may be given.
Mr. BALLANTYNlE: The hon. member has stated the case fairly and correctly. There is no doubt that the Department of Marine ought to have more icebreakers than it has; at any rate, it ought to have ships of sufficient power to break the ice, especially at the ports of Shelburne and Lockeport. We are short of boats of that kind, but I will take into my very best consideration the remarks which the hon. member has made. Every effort will be made to have in that locality when necessary a vessel of sufficient strength to break the ice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I referred a moment ago to the fair-wages resolution which had been adopted toy the House. I have obtained a copy of the resolution, and I find that I was correct in saying that it was adopted twenty years ago. The resolution was introduced on March 22, 1900, and passed on July 17. It reads as follows:
That all Government contracts should contain such conditions as will prevent abuses which may arise from the subletting of such contracts, and that every effort should be made to secure the payment of such wages as are generally accepted as current in each trade for competent workmen in the district where the work is carried out, and that this House cordially concurs in such policy, and deems it the duty of the Government to take immediate steps to give effect thereto.
It is hereby declared that the work to which the foregoing policy shall apply includes not only work undertaken by the Government itself, but also all works aided by grant of Dominion public funds.
During the years that I had to do with the Department of Labour, I remember, the department used to receive from the different spending departments of the Government requests that the fair-wage officer of the department should go to localities in which public work was to be undertaken and ascertain the current rates of wages. Then,'when tenders were called for, a schedule was attached as part of the specifications fixing current rates of wages, and in the case of clothing contracts, a minimum wage was inserted in the contract. That is

the manner in which the different departments sought to carry out the terms of this resolution. Does the minister's department award contracts in compliance with this resolution, or has the resolution been allowed to lapse during the war, like a good many other things that were done for the protection of labour and the protection of public funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That system has been and is toeing followed in connection with what little purchasing is lift in the hands of the Department of Marine. As the hon. gentleman knows, practically all purchases are now made, as they were during the war, by the War Purchasing Commission. I cannot say for the moment whether the War Purchasing Commission are familiar with the resolution referred to by the hon. member; in any case, it will be my pleasure to see that they are informed of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In connection with the repairing of ships, and the like, does the minister require the officers of his department to see that schedules are inserted in the contracts specifying the wages that are to be paid to. the men engaged in the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I could quite understand the necessity of just such a statute as that twenty years ago, and I would take no exception whatever to it now; but the highest scale of wages is always paid. There has been, and there exists to-day, a great shortage of skilled and unskilled labour, and the highest price is always paid for any woik performed by the Government or by shipbuilders repairing ships for the Government. They are forced to pay the current scale of wages otherwise they would be unable to obtain men.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is just .one feature that I would draw to the attention of the minister in that connection. Where tenders are called for and contracts awarded to the lowest tenderer, unless some schedule is inserted specifying the current wage, if there happens to be, amongst the number who tender, a contractor who, perhaps, is not as considerate of his labour as the others, and is prepared to sweat his labour, such a contractor gets an undue advantage by virtue of his meanness over other contractors who wish to deal in a fair manner with their labour. That is the reason why I think that, even at a time such as the present when labour may be scarce, it is desirable to follow rigid-

ly a resolution of the House in the particulars mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My department, of
course, is aware of the prevailing wage for every contract that is let, that is, the wages that are being paid for a contract that has been let to any particular firm. So far as possible, we try to see that fair wages are paid, and I have not heard of any complaints.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):
speechtext:
I want to draw the attention of the minister to a question of considerable interest in my constituency, and I think it will come under this item. About ten or twelve years ago, it was found advisable to maintain a vessel at Canso in case of accident to the winter fishing. My hon. friend is aware that in winter snow storms occur very suddenly. You may have a bright clear morning when the fleet goes out and before three or four o'clock in the afternoon there may be a severe snow storm which would make it difficult for the boats to get back to land. Canso may be said to be the headquarters of the winter fishing. I think it is the only port in Nova (Scotia where winter fishing is carried on through the whole of the months of December and January until the ice is moving so much in February and March that fishing has to be abandoned; but winter fishing is a very profitable part of the fishing industry in that locality. It is to some extent a new industry, because years ago the fishermen never attempted to carry on winter fishing; they closed up their business in the late fall and pulled up their boats, and nothing more was done until the spring. But it was discovered that haddock fishing is better in the winter than at any other time, and that it is a profitable branch of the fishing industry. During the Administration of Six Wilfrid Laur-ier, this matter was represented to the department over which my hon. friend presides, and at that time a boat known as the " 33 " was used for that purpose. It was one of the Scotch drifters that was brought out from the Old Country for experimental purposes, and it served the purpose very well. It was kept under steam at Canso, so that if a storm came up during the day, the " 33 " could go out to the fleet, and the rest of the boats could follow the leader .into the harbour. There have been cases where it looked as if a very serious loss of life might have taken place on an occasion of that kind. I understand the " .33 " has been sold and is no longer one
of the Government's boats. Has the minister abandoned the idea of protecting the winter fishing, or is it the policy of the department to continue the practice that has been observed for so many years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will be good enough to bring the question up again when I am on my Fishery Estimates, I will look into the matter and I shall be prepared to give him a more definite reply than what I am able to do at the moment. He is quite correct in stating that the " 33" has been sold.

I am not So much concerned about the " 33 " being sold. I think it would have been better if she had not been sold, but my inquiry is, whether the department has any plan to continue that service, or whether the minister favours the continuance of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
will realize that I could not- give him a direct answer until I have an opportunity of looking into what has been done during the past and the circumstances as they exist to-day. I will, with pleasure, look into the matter and shall be prepared to give a definite answer when the Fishery Estimates are under the consideration of the committee.

I should like to ask the , minister a question somewhat along the line mentioned by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) as to the uniformity of wages on ships in the employ of or owned by the Government. There is, as the minister knows, a ship called the Tyrrian under the control of and owned by the Department of Public Works and she has quite a crew. Her particular business is the repairing of cables around the coast -for instance the cable between the Magdalen Islands and Cape North. Her crew are continually complaining that they are not receiving the same rate of wages as men employed on similar ships in the Marine Service, and they are continually writing me letters along that line. What is the scale of wages, say on the Montcalm, for the captain and officers down to the men?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A conference was
recently held between the Department of Railways and Canals, the Department of Public Works and of the Department of Marine and of the Naval Service in order to see if a uniform scale of wages could not be arrived at. Heretofore, there has not been that unity of purpose, and I know that a variation exists in the scale of wages paid

in the various departments, but now we are endeavouring to frame a uniform scale. The rate of wages paid on the steamer Montcalm is as follows: The captain gets $140 a month; the first officer, $100; the second officer, $75; and the chief engineer, $130. I am unable to state what wages are paid on the steamer to which the hon. member has just referred, because that belongs to the Department of Public Works.
Mr. iMcKENZIE:	I did not expect the
minister would have that information. There is a chief steward on "The Tyrrian." Is there such an officer on "The Montcalm," and if so, what salary does he get?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes; $70 a month.
(Mr. CHISHOLM:	I understand the
minister is in thfe habit of employing steamers for icebreaking purposes. Last winter he employed a steamer from my part of the country to go up to the southern coast of Nova Scotia. What is the policy of the department when steamers so employed get wrecked? Does the department pay for the damages? I think this vessel was called the "Kinburn."

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am not aware that any such steamer was hired by the Department of Marine.
Mr. iCHLSMGLM:	What department of
the Government would employ a steamer of that kind?
That is very difficult to answer, but I will endeavour to find out. It was not the Department of Marine.

The reason I ask is
that I know this steamer was employed in breaking .ice around one of the harbours on the southern coast of Nova Scotia, and I think a second steamer was engaged from the port of Halifax. I think both s'teamers were wrecked. They were a failure, and could not do very much work as they were not fitted for that purpose. What I want to find out is whether the Government pays for the damages ships suffer while so employed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will endeavour

The War Purchasing Commission does not purchase supplies for the 'Government ships of the Marine Department; the steward purchases supplies by tender.

supplies does the War Purchasing 'Commission purchase for the Marine 'Department? Does it purchase provisions of any kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:

purchase oils and coal, but never provisions.
'Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR:	The commission
has made a report to the House, which they call a memorandum, regarding the proposed Purchasing Board for Canada. In report they have a table showing what they have been buying during the past year. The 'Marine Department is men-Moned in connection with purchases as fo1-lows: provisions to the extent of $115,759, dry goods $17,597, hardware $213,911, mechanical supplies $27,220, scientific supplies $5,573, miscellaneous $126,052; total $506,1'12. Can the minister tell us what these supplies were for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can only say that the War Purchasing Commission has not bought any supplies for the Government ships of the 'Marine Department. They may have been in error in saying "Marine." They may have meant "Naval Service." The War Purchasing Commission has nothing whatever to do with the buying of provisions for the Government ships of the Marine Department.

Are we to understand
that this highly efficient and most capable body, the War Purchasing Commission, has charged the Marine Department with some $500,000 of goods that they never received? I would ask the President of the Pirivy Oouneil to take particular note of that, because for some two or three years his specialty has been to preach about the great reforms that will be accomplished by having a commission of this kind. Of course, a new system of book-keeping may have been devised, by which one department is charged for the goods received by another, making confusion worse confounded. I am very glad this information has been brought out, as it must be of interest to the hon. gentleman who is the father and godfather and grandfather of the legislation with respect to the Purchasing Board.
