Does this item cover the salaries of the men who are engaged as teachers and examiners of masters and mates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. It is for the examiners, stenographers, office rent, telephone, travelling, etc.

I do not know that I have ever had the opportunity of bringing to the notice of the minister some particulars with respect to the examiner and teacher at the station in my own town. We have a very respectable gentleman there, well advanced in years, but quite capable as a teacher. He is an old shipmaster and deep sea man. He is not now able to do any hard work, as he has been the victim of rheumatism, but he is a capable teacher and is very bright. He depends entirely for his living, I believe, on what he gets from the Government for his work as examiner and teacher. His salary is very -small. I should like /to find out what it is, -and if there is any chance of increasing it, *and whether it has been increased within the last few years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Does the minister not think that under present conditions $300 is a very small allowance for a man who has to support a family? He must be a first-class man or the position cannot be properly filled. It is useless to put any man in charge of a school of that kind unless he knows his business, and I am sure that Captain Sutherland is a first-class mariner. The station is an important one where there are a number of seamen, and in the summer time quite a number of people residing in the town go to it. It is desirable to keep the school up, and I trust that the minister will give this man some consideration. Instead of $300 he should be receiving $600.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I overlooked the fact that Captain Sutherland, in addition to the $300 which he receives, is also given $250 for his lectures, and I am informed that very many examinations do not take place at that point, the total number during the past year having been eight. The captain's total remuneration amounts to $550.
Well, it requires only $50 more to bring it up to the modest standard I -suggest.
The minister has mentioned several stations. Is there at each of these stations a school where navigation is taught?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Investigations into wrecks, $12,300.
What is this item for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Whenever a wreck occurs it is at once reported to the Marine Department, and the Wreck Commissioner, Captain Demers, is sent to hold an investigation. The amount I am asking the committee to vote is to provide for the Wreck Commissioner's salary, travelling expenses, and all expenditures connected with the wrecks that occur during the year. If it is discovered that the captain or the pilot is at fault, the Wreck Commissioner has power to suspend him or to cancel his certificate altogether, or for a certain period, as he sees fit, according to the gravity of the case.
The minister cannot mean that Captain Demers is sent to investigate every wreck.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: So far as it is possible to do so. I would not expect him to investigate the wreck of a tug, but in the case of a steamer of any size he certainly would make an investigation.
In the case of these wrecks that do not come within his purview, what officer is employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Any officer who may be delegated by the Government to hold such investigations. But in the case of wrecks of vessels of considerable tonnage, such as sea-going vessels, it is the duty of the Wreck Commissioner to make investigations.

Has the department any policy for providing suitable wrecking craft on the Atlantic coast? We have a merchant marine in which we have invested almost 6100,000,000, and on the Atlantic coast we have no suitable craft for salvaging, and no proper appliances for assisting vessels that are wrecked. In view of the fact that we are often tied up in the shipping business, I think it would be wise to make provision for suitable appliances in order that we might be able to attend properly to wrecked vessels, and save them whenever possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government
have a wrecking plant on the Pacific coast and one at Quebec. It has none at Halifax

or on the Atlantic coast, because there are several good wrecking firms in the city of Halifax, which are quite able to look after any wrecks that occur, without calling on the Government for assistance,
Has the Dominion Coal Company any appliances of this kind, or did they in the past receive any subsidy from the Government for this work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They did receive a subsidy in the past, but it is no longer given.
Expenses of schools of navigation, $8,000.
Who conducts the School of Navigation in Charlottetown, P.E.I., and what does it cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a private school in Charlottetown which the Government does not support.
Is this 68,000 to provide for the same service a-s is included in the items we have already passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The item which we have already passed has reference to schools for the examination of those candidates who come up to qualify as masters and mates. The present item provides for schools where those men are taught the rules of navigation. Schools are located at St. John, N.B., Halifax, Yarmouth, Quebec, Kingston, Vancouver, North Sydney, and Col-lingwood.
There is no school at Charlottetown?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Only a private
school.

Does the department give any assistance to private schools? I know that several seamen who were anxious to study navigation applied to a master mariner to open a school in Prince Edward Island and I should like to know if it is the policy of the department to assist private schools in any way.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not the policy of the department to give assistance to private schools.
They are doing nothing in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

Some of this money, I presume, goes to the technical school in the city of Halifax. I understand that navigation is taught in the provincial technical school in that city. How much money is

the Government paying to that institution? And are we getting a return for it? Along the same line, and with a view to economy,
I suppose we will cut down largely in the expenditure upon the unnecessary education that we have been bestowing upon these masters and mates. We have passed legislation which relieves the minister of any necessity of providing instruction or examination for masters and mates and there should be retrenchment along that line. The minister will probably tell us what saving he expects to make by reason of the reduction that has been made in the requirements with reference to masters and mates. Whether he will answer that question or not, perhaps he will give us some information as to what is being done at this School of Technology and whether he thinks it necessary to assist education in this way.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In regard to the
Halifax school; the Department of Marine pays Captain John Symonds, instructor, $100 per month. That is the only contribution the Government makes to that school which is connected with the Halifax University. I have no hesitation in answering the hon. gentleman's other question in regard to the service certificates that may be granted to masters and mates. Masters and mates have to come up for examination just the same as they always did, and therefore the expense remains the same.

I had supposed that
both of these examinations would be conducted over the long distance telephone and that there would be a saving in travelling expenses and that sort of thing. Does the minister think it necessary to appoint an officer whose special business it will be to examine into this' new position? I am quite serious about this. I am not aware that he himself is a nautical man but there may be some nautical men in his department. I think it is highly desirable that there should be somebody who is very keen and capable, and who has a knowledge of marine affairs, to examine these men coming up under the new law.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have three examiners now in the province of Nova Scotia and if the department thinks they are not sufficient we will increase the number, because no man will be granted a certificate unless he can pass the necessary rigid examination.

The expense of the schools of navigation is $8,000 a year and that of the examiners and mates $18,000, making 103*
a total of $26,000. Last year 207 masters and mates passed the examination. Twenty-six thousand dollars for 207 masters and mates represents an expenditure of over $100 each. What benefit has the country got from this? What contribution are the masters and mates making towards this expense? Are they paying anything to attend these schools, or any fee to be allowed to try the examination, or is the country paying everything?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is only a small fee of $5 for a mate and $10 for a master. The figure 207 that I gave was only for ocean-going and. coasting steamers. If I had given the figures for the inland and minor waters the total would be 344. Now that the Government are the owners of such a large mercantile marine, and as we have some twenty-five or thirty ships already in commission, if it were not for the desire to economize in every direction, the 'Government would be justified in spending a much larger sum for these schools and for the examination of masters and mates, because I am sure I am expressing the
10	p.m. view of all hon. members when I say that we would like to see not only 'Government ships but all ships under Canadian register manned as far as possible by Canadians. We are offering this tuition at such an extremely low figure to encourage Canadians to take up a seafaring career.

The extraordinary thing about these figures is that it costs $8,000 to teach the men navigation and $18,000 to examine them. I have had some experience in educational matters, as I was an educationalist for a part of my life. The expensive thing is the education and not the examination. If the minister would reverse the process and spend $18,000 in teaching the subject and $8,000 on the examination of the students after they are taught, it would be more reasonable. Will the minister explain why he expends so much money on examinations and so little on education?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A very large number who come up for examination for masters and mates do not attend schools, and that explains the difference between the two items.
To provide for the temporary relief of distressed seamen and to cover the expenses of shipping forms, $3,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When sailors are in distress owing to their ships having been wrecked, the department 'brings them to the nearest port and pays their expense. Sometimes we have to provide clothing for them.
Was anything spent on *this item last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The amount was
$2,905 to the end of March.
This does not include medical attendance; that comes under another item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That comes under another item.

I understand the practice to be that any moneys expended in this way aTe recoverable from the owner of the vessel. Supposing a ship is wrecked on the Nova Scotia coast and $1,000 has to be expended by the Department in looking after the seamen, is there not-an. arrangement by which that money is recoverable from the shipowner?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, the hon. member is quite right, and we do recover wherever we can.
My hon. friend mentions English ships. Doe$ it not include our own ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Registration of shipping, $6,000.

A proposal was made recently to appoint a surveyor or a measurer-I do not know just what is the official title-for measuring ships, at Isaacs Harbour, which is some distance away from any registry available for the shipbuilders in that locality. I would like to know if anything has been done in that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter is still
under consideration.

My hon. friend will probably have in his office the facts showing the necessity of having some one appointed at that point. It is some seventy miles from Canso, and a longer distance from the next office westerly, in fact, I do not think there is any registry office between Canso and Halifax, and that district is very badly off for some one to examine and measure small vessels built in the locality. It becomes difficult sometimes to find an officer, and as he has to travel long distances to do the work unnecessary expense is incurred by the shipbuilders. Under the present regulations the builder has to bear

the expenses of the survey. It is important that this accommodation should be given to the people of that coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will be very glad to look into the matter.
Mr. 'CHISHOLM : There is a certain class of officers in the service whose duty it is to do this work. Who are they? For instance, in my own constituency, if we have a small vessel to be measured, to whom do we apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a particular class of men engaged in that work, and my hon. friend would apply to the collector of customs for a measuring surveyor to be sent.
Then you have officers known ajs measuring surveyors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Is this a highly technical profession?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Fairly so.

In cases such as my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) has referred to- and I have a similar case in my own constituency-it has often occurred to me that if it i)S not a highly technical process some of the collectors of customs might do the work. The collectors at Cheticamp and Mar-garee, I understand, do this work and report to the department, so saving the expense and affording great convenience to the people.	-	!

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, quite a number of customs officials do that work.
Supposing I want to have one of those officers authorized to do this work, what should I do?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member would apply to the customs house if he wanted an official to make a survey. If he wanted some one appointed, that power is vested in the Governor in Council.

Some years ago we had an official of this kind in the city of Sydney, Mr. Charles Hill, whom no doubt my hon. friend and the deputy minister will remember. He died; and I am not aware of anybody having been appointed in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. F. I. Stewart has been appointed.
Inspection of live stock shipments, $3y00'0.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: What are the duties of these live stock inspectors, and where is their work carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Their duties are to see that suitable accommodation is provided for the shipment of cattle and that proper precautions are taken in reference to their health and safe carraige.
At what ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Montreal.
Is no provision made for inspection anywhere else?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Apart from the shipments that go out of the port of Montreal, we have practically no cattle shipments abroad.
None from St. John?

None, for instance,
from North Sydney to Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If there are any live stock shipments they must be very small in number. I thought it questionable whether we should retain this vote even for such an important port as Montreal, but after looking into the matter to-day I think we are justified in continuing it there, but I do not think we would be justified in establishing similar inspection at any other port.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: At a recent session it was brought to the attention of the minister that cattle shippers were complaining oi the lack of space for cattle shipments in our Government merchant marine, which shipments had in consequence to be diverted to the port of New York. If we are not going to have any cattle space in our merchant marine, the question very naturally arises: Why should we have the inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have taken the matter up with the officials of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine to see if they cannot equip their ships to carry live stock. The Canadian Pacific, the White Star, the Cunard, and a number of other steamship lines carry live stock, and that is the reason we have to keep these inspectors at Montreal.

It is quite evident that the minister is not familiar with the trade of the Maritime Provinces. The port of North Sydney in its live stock shipments compares more than favourably with the port of Montreal.
That is what I thought.

We have an
official in the city of Sydney, Doctor Thurston, a very capable veterinary surgeon,
who established a very fine reeord overseas. He is in some way connected with the Government service, but I do not know exactly what his office is. 'Sydney is seventeen miles by railway and five miles by water from North Sydney, and sometimes it is very inconvenient to be obliged to wait until Doctor Thurston can come to North Sydney to make inspections. I would not like to ask for anything that would in any way interfere with the pay or status of Doctor Thurston, because he is a very capable official and a returned soldier with a very fine record, but I would like to ask the minister to consider the advisability of appointing an officer at North Sydney for this work. It certainly would be a convenience to shippers of cattle via North Sydney to have a man there who would do the work at once and avoid any delays.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The officer the
hon. member refers to is a health of animals officer, under the Department of Agriculture. This item pertains to the equipment of ships for the safety of live stock on long sea voyages.
To continue subsidies for wrecking plants- Quebec and British Columbia, $35,000.

This is an
item of considerable importance; possibly it had better stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Very well.
It is understood that .any member who is absent may discuss ,any other items than the two which are reserved-even the items that have been passed.
No.

That has been the
practice in the past.

If there is
any doubt in the mind of any one, I think that a reference to Hansard to-morrow will show that I pointed out that we did not care to block any of these items and that if the minister was willing to allow a subsequent discussion of any of the items that we might pass to-night in connection with the items that were reserved, we would allow them to pass. The minister gave that undertaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is right.
Item stands.
Unforeseen expenses, $5,000.

Is there any way in which these unforeseen expenses

are_ accounted for? I notice that the Customs Department have an appropriation for an amount to be paid to the Department of Justice " to be disbursed by and *accounted for to it, for secret preventive service." I do not observe any vote in other departments for unforeseen expenses of that sort.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The unforeseen expenses for 1919-20 included $943.65 to P. S. Ross and Sons, auditors, of Montreal. I sent- them down to St. John to make an audit of the books there, because at that time I was introducing a Bill to nationalize the harbour of St. John. Then there are other accounts for printing and for professional services of Mr. R. V. Sinclair. The total was $1,745.68.

Some of the
amounts expended last year as " unforeseen expenses " would appear to be really not unforeseen, such as printing and stationery; printing of the report on the harbour of Vancouver. These items amount to $273.97. I see no reason why expenditure of that kind should be put down as " unforeseen."
i Mr. BALLANTYNE:	The amount for
printing is very small. The payment to P. S. Ross and Sons could not have been foreseen. That was the largest amount; the next largest was: Bank of Montreal, deposit security, $500.
I see that H. R. Silver, of Halifax, was paid $298.07 for travelling expenses and disbursements in connection with Ship's Licensing Committee. What was that committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
During the war
it was thought desirable to require ships clearing from Halifax to have a license to do so. That requirement does not now exist.
Mr. J. H, SINCLAIR:	Did this officer
grant the licenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. All he got
was his travelling expenses.
Amounts required for two motor patrol vessels for buoy and lighthouse service in British Columbia, $150,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That item
might stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be glad to let it stand if the leader of the Opposition iso desires, but it is not a controversial matter. It is a re-vote from last year.

How much was spent
last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Nothing.
Where are these boats to be built?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In British. Columbia.
What will be their size and horse-power?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: 95 feet long; 100 horse-power.	,
How many motor boats of that character has the minister now in this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These are the first that the department has ordered for the buoy service.
Is it intended that these boats shall be provided for the Atlantic coast as well as the Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, not now.

Why are these
boats provided for the Pacific coast and not for the Atlantic?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are inland
waters in British Columbia upon which these small boats may operate. Their use would not be feasible upon the Atlantic coast.

Will they be of
wood or steel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Wood.
River St. Lawrence ship channel-maintenance and operating dredging fleet, $478,000.
How many dredges are already in operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Last year we had
the following dredges in operation on the St. Lawrence ship channel: 3 elevator dredges with tugs; I suction self-propelling hopper dredge; 1 self-propelling coal barge; 2 inspection sweeping steamers; 2 stone elevators; floating shop; 1 rock cutter.
Does the Government *antemplate the construction of any new dredges for the St. Lawrence channel this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I wish it were possible to give the hon. member an affirmative answer. But we are trying to keep down expenses; we are not going to construct any new dredges, although they are needed.
Mr, DECHENE:	I asked the question
because I was informed by a mariner that

there was at Sorel a dredge all ready to be put into service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is at Sorel a dredge partially completed by the Vickers Company, but we are not going ahead with if as we are trying to economize.
Do all the dredges belong to the department, or are any owned by private companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are all owned by the Government.
Is any work done by companies as such?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No.
Mr. DECHENSe : How much money has already been spent in the construction of that dredge?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I should say at
least $100,000; but it is a very expensive dredge, and the question of extras comes up now owing to the fact that my predecessor, quite properly, owing to the war, gave instructions to the Vickers Company at Montreal to discontinue work on this dredge.
I have since given instructions not to proceed with it because it would cost several hundreds of thousands of dollars, and I do not think the financial condition of the country would warrant us in spending such a large amount of money at the present time.
Where are these dredges repaired now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At Sorel.

I remember the time
when the Department of Public Works did all the dredging. Does the Department of Marine do all the dredging of the St. Lawrence now, or is there a line of demarcation between the work done by the two departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Department of
Marine do all the dredging of the St. Lawrence ship channel from Montreal to a considerable distance below Quebec, something around 342 miles.

Would the minister
give us some idea of the system followed in connection with this dredging? We in the Maritime Provinces are very much interested in this artery of commerce, the St. Lawrence, and should like to know the system that is followed in the expenditure of this money. Is it expended in keeping the channel clear of any possible impediment -that might come into the channel, or
is it used for deepening and widening the channel, or what might be called new work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The annual expenditure' under this vote is for deepening and widening the channel, and at the present time we have at low water thirty feet of water in the channel from Montreal to the sea; but dredging is being continued in order to reach a depth of thirty-five feet, and the curves are also being widened.

: Once work of this character is completed down to thirty or thirty-five feet, does it .remain clear or does the minister find that he has to go over the work and scrape the channel again shortly after the work has been done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The channel has
remained clear and will remain clear entirely throughout the year. There is a place called Cap Madeleine where it silts ,in a little.	.

Was the depth of thirty feet maintained, for instance during the last fifteen years? I understand that the St. Lawrence channel had an average depth of thirty feet from Montreal to Quebec. The minister says that once the depth is reached, that is, when the channel is dug, if I may use that word, it remains clear, with the exception of this spot that he mentioned. Then the whole work is being done at this very spot.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
What is the object of the other dredging?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The department intends to dredge the St. Lawrence ship channel to a depth of thirty-five feet, and we have not accomplished that yet by any means. We have thirty feet now at low water. At certain parts of the channel, for instance, at a place called Cap la Roch, rock is being taken out, and we are widening the channel at the curves because the steamers are becoming larger all the time.

All the way to
Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
What effect does the deepening of the channel have on the water? I saw in the press a statement that when you deepened the channel down below the water above Is apt to become shallower.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That statement
has often been made, but I have never been able to find any real foundation foT it.

In the opinion of the
minister how long will it take to reach a depth of thirty-five feet between Quebec and Montreal at the rate work is going on now, year after year? I understand the channel was thirty feet deep fifteen years ago, and every summer we have been spending half a million dollars, more or less, on dredging and it seems we have not made any progress in that regard. The minister mentions now that the channel is still thirty feet deep.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
is quite right. The channel has been thirty feet in depth for a number of years; but we have to continue the work until we have the channel dredged to a depth of thirty-five feet, and as longer steamers are constantly being built, we have to widen the channel at various points. I do not think the work will ever be absolutely completed; but just how many years it will take to dredge the channel to a depth of thirty-five feet, and to make it the width that the Government think it ought to be, depends altogether on the generosity of Parliament. We used to have an appropriation as large as $1,000,000 for this work; now it has been reduced to $478,000. The depth of water during the several months of the season of 1019 was as follows:	In May, 39 feet 7
inches; in June, 36 feet 7 inches; in July, 33 feet 5 inches; in August, 32 feet 4 inches; in September, 32 feet 3 inches; in October, 32 feet 8 inches; in November, 33 feet 5 inches.

It is a very big undertaking to deepen the St. Lawrence channel five additional feet. Has the minister taken advice as to what the total cost would be? I presume that Parliament is in sympathy with the proposal as this is one of the great works of the country, and we all look forward to the day when the St. Lawrence channel will be thirty-five feet deep, but I should like to have some idea of what it is going to cost us.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Dredging to the
extent of 29,000,000 cubic yards has yet to be done on the channel to bring it to a depth of thirty-five feet.
M,r. BELAND:	What does it cost per
cubic yard now? It used to cost 25 cents per cubic yard twenty years ago.
I do not want the minister to answer a question like that unless he has an estimate made by a competent engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have here an estimate by competent engineers of the department.

How much of that
estimate is rock? Does the engineer report that rock excavations will have to be made in order to obtain that depth?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have encountered rock at Cap la Roch. We have a width there of from 500 to 550 feet, whereas formerly it was 300 to 400 feet. The total number of cubic yards removed during the season of 1919 was 88,655. The channel was deepened to 30 feet in 1897.

I understand that during the last six or seven years the Government has been building a new deep water channel from the north shore below the Island of Orleans down to the Lower Traverse. How is that work progressing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are seven miles of the north channel yet to be dredged. The new dredge that was referred to a moment ago is now lying partially completed at Sorel. It will have to be completed before the seven miles can be dredged.
Is it sand or rock that is being taken out?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Neither, it is what we call heavy boulders.
To what depth has the channel been dredged?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: About 20 feet, for a distance of over eight miles.
Will no more dredging be done until the new dredge is completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will go on so far as our present plant will permit, but we cannot complete the north channel until the new dredge is finished.
Is this new channel to avoid dangerous places?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, there is quite a number that will be avoided.

Some years ago, about 1912 or 1914, some dredging was done from the wharves at Montmagny to the main channel. Dredging was done to a depth of six feet outside the wharves, but the work was never completed to the main channel.
Is it intended to complete this channel for small boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That dredging
comes under the Department of Public

Works. We only look after the main ship channel.

I should like to suggest to the minister that possibly it is not wise for this Government and this country to enter into a race with the shipbuilding concerns of the world and go on deepening the St. Lawrence river. I am very anxious indeed that we should have a very spacious entrance to and along the St. Lawrence river, but larger ships are continually being built. Some years ago a ship with a draught of 25 or 28 feet was considered a very large one; it is a large ship to-day. I gather that the minister is now trying to accommodate ships with a draught of 35 feet. It is only a matter of a short time before a much larger ship than that will be built, and then his 35 feet will not be much good unless he goes on dredging still deeper. We are also told that aerial navigation is going to be a factor in the commerce of this country in a very short time. Is it wise, therefore, for us to be spending so much on deepening the St. Lawrence river when we cannot hope to keep pace with the increasing size of ships? Would it not be better for the Canadian people and more helpful for the commerce of Canada if we had a 30-foot waterway from the Atlantic to Port Arthur, for instance, then a 35-foot channel up to Montreal only. I submit that thought to the minister. I think the question of a waterway from Port Arthur to the sea is becoming more and more important every day, and I think it is well worthy of consideration whether we should not construct such a waterway rather than go on deepening the St. Lawrence. It is quite possible that within the next ten or fifteen years, and I say this in all seriousness, the commerce of this country will be largely carried on by aerial navigation, and we may then think ourselves foolish in having spent so much money on deepening the St Lawrence. I feel I am on perfectly firm ground from the national standpoint when I say that it is of more importance to the Canadian people to have this 30-foot waterway from Port Arthur to the sea than a 35-foot channel from the sea to Montreal.
The minister was going to give me an estimate of the total cost of deepening the St. Lawrence river to 35 feet.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is rather difficult to give an estimate. We have the cost for last year per cubic yard, and we know how much is going to be dredged, but the costs,
of course, vary from year to year. I should say, roughly, about $20,000,000.
What does the dredging cost now per cubic yard?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Elevator dredge No. 2, 73 cents per cubic yard; No. 3, 36 cents; No. 5, 73 cents; No. 8, 41 cents.
Is the difference due to different classes of material or to the different dredges?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Of course, the material varies, and the cost varies with the different dredges. It depends on the material and the bed of the river.
How many men are engaged on these dredges.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: From eighteen to twenty.
Are all of these men receiving bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The bonus is given only to those who are not getting the prevailing rate of wages, but we are readjusting matters now and shall pay them all a certain wage which will be equal to their former scale of wages together with bonus.
During the winter are these men laid off completely?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are laid off
during the winter months.
They do not get any salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Are all these dredges on the St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On the St. Lawrence only.
What do the men do in the winter season?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are laid up at Sorel?
Are they not on the payroll in winter at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

Why do you make a difference between men engaged on dredges and those who work on steamers. The men on the steamers are paid half wages in winter, and I do not see why the men on the dredges should not be treated in the same way.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry to have conveyed the impression that the entire

crew of the steamers were given half-pay [DOT]during winter. Only the officers and the chief engineer receives half-pay. The rest of the crew do not draw any pay.
Is that the same on the dredges?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. The officers and engineers on the dredges do not get anything in winter.
Why the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Because the officers on the dredges are entirely in a different category from the officers on the steamers. The captain on the dredge does his work quite well, but he does not need to know as much about navigation as the captain of a ship.

Some of the government steamers do not go very far from shore, and it does not need any great knowledge of navigation to man them. Two ships stationed at Quarantine do not go very far from shore. They sail between Quebec and Quarantine, some thirty miles, and the dredges have a good deal of hard work to do. The engineers on the dredges have to keep their engines in good order, and they do probably more work than those on some of the steamers. I do not see therefore why there should be such a distinction between men who are doing practically the same kind of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has never been the custom to pay men on the dredges in winter, and I am quite sure hon. members would not have this Government establish a precedent now.

Is it intended to continue the bonus system during the present year? I see by the Auditor General's report that the bonus is nearly as large as the wages of the men. It is an extraordinary way of paying ordinary workmen to give them so much wages and a bonus amounting to pretty nearly the same sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not the intention of the department to continue the bor/us system, but simply to pay the prevailing wages.

Is it the intention of the minister to do more dredging in front of the Quarantine wharves, so that big steamers, instead of being obliged to anchor outside, will be able to come in and unload at the wharves? At present the steamers are bound to anchor in the channel, and

this involves a great deal of inconvenience, and expense in unloading in mid-stream. If dredging were done at the wharves it would save time and a good deal of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I must ask my hon. friend to take up this question when the Public Works Estimates are under consideration. It is a subject that does not appertain to the Marine Department.

I would suppose that the Minister of Marine would have a good deal to do with the matter o-f dredging. If this work were done it would mean a great saving of time and would be a great convenience. There is no doubt about the urgent necessity of this icebreaker and I would like to get the item passed in order that tenders may be called and if at all possible have the icebreaker ready for next winter.
For the maintenance and improvements of the Sorel shipyard, shops and offices as well as operating expenses, $65,000.
Are things going on at this shipyard in the same old way, and is the same work being done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The operations carried on at the Sorel shipyards are very much restricted in comparison with former years. We are not doing as much work; we are trying to follow a policy of economy.
Will the minister give us an idea as to how much of this money is to be expended in rebuilding or improving shops, and how much will be spent for operating purposes?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I would suggest to the minister that we allow this item to stand until hon. members who desire to speak on it are present. The hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) intimated to me a desire to say something in reference to this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Very well; I have no objection to letting the item stand.
Item stands.
To provide for the construction of an icebreaking steamer to be used on the River St. Lawrence, $2,000,000.
Should we not let this item stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no objection to leaving this item, but the hon. members from Quebec city, who are most interested in it, have expressed their approval. There is no doubt that this icebreaker is needed.
I should like to make as much progress as

possible in view of the fact that we have already let two large items stand.
What kind of a ship are you going to build and where are you going to build it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The ship will be similar to the. "J. D. Hazen" that was built some years ago. Just where she will be built, it will toe gratifying to the leader of the Opposition to know, can only be determined after public tenders have been called. The length of the ship will be 275 [DOT]feet, breadth 57 feet 6 inches, depth to mould 32 feet, draught 19 feet 3 inches, deadweight 950 tons, horse-power 8,000 and complement of officers and men about 90.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like to remind the minister of his promise that he will see, in connedtion with this particular expenditure, if it is possible to have a vessel which will serve the double purpose of an icebreaker in winter and a car ferry in sumnner. If he can see his way to arrange that it will save a great amount of expense in the end in the matter of a second car ferry and it will be much appreciated by the people of Prince Edward Island.
Will thalt ship be much more powerful than those we have to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Many times.
Will it keep the channel open all winter to Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
She could of course go up and down but I do not know whether it is feasible to attempt to keep the river open.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The Hon. N. W. ROWELL moved the second reading of Bill No. 20 to amend the Opium and Drug Act.

We had thought the House was going to adjourn after these Estimates. I do nolt see why the second reading of this Bill should be taken up now. I have a lot of letters and
11	p.m. communications on this Opium and Drug Act and I would like to say something about it.' The President of the Privy Council is repeating his old trick of taking measures of (this kind up on Friday night when many hon. members are absent from the House. I think he ought not to try and force this Bill through its second reading to-night.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had waited he might noit have spoken with the feeling that he has manifested in his remarks. It is not my intention to ask the House to proceed with the second reading to-night but as I intend when the House gets into committee to submit some important amendments to the Bill I thought it would facilitate the consideration of the Bill if I put on record to-night what these amendments are, so that hon. members will have them in Hansard and know the character of the amendments before we proceed with the discussion of the second reading. I therefore arranged with the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. King) that the second reading should be formally moved to-night in order that I might put upon Hansard the amendments I intend to ask the committee to consider when the Bill comes 'before it.
And then the second reading will be carried.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I do not ask that the second reading be carried. I had hoped to save the time of the House and to contribute ito the convenience of members by putting these amendments on record.
We appreciate it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I knew my hon. friend would.
The general rule is that when you move the second reading of a Bill it is read a second time. I did not know about any private agreement.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When the resolution upon which the Bill is founded was before the House I explained that the object of the Bill was to enable the Government to carry out its obligation under the International Opium Convention which was signed at The Hague in 1912, and went into effect in January of this year by virtue of the provisions of the Treaty of Peace. Representations have been made by the druggists of the country in reference to the form of the Bill. These representations have been considered and when the Bill goes into committee I intend submitting two amendments. After reading these to the House I intend moving the adjournment of the debate. The amendments will be in the form of two new subsections, first, a subsection which will repeal the existing subsection (1) of section (5) of the Opium and Drug Act of 1911, and will substitute for it a new section which is identical with the original section except that it leaves out all reference to the preservation of a record of the sales and

changes the penalties. The record o>f sales is dealt with in subsection (5-A) in a fuller and more comprehensive way and therefore I propose to leave out those portions of section (5). As the penalties in section (5) and section (5-A) differ, I intend making the penalties under section (5) of the Act of 1911 the same as are now proposed under section (5-A) in the present Bill in order that there may be no confusion in prosecution and no question as to whether, a party is being prosecuted under section (5) or section (5-A). It is thought desirable to have the penalties the same. Therefore the amendment is:
(4) Section 5, subsection 1, of the said Act is1 hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor:
" Any person who deals in any drug, who gives, sells or furnishes any drug to any person other than a duly authorized and practising physician, veterinary surgeon or dentist, or to a bona fide wholesale druggist, or to a druggist carrying on business in a bona fide drug store, and any druggist who gives, sells or furnishes any drug except upon a written order or prescription signed by a duly authorized and practising physician, veterinary surgeon or dentist, or who, without the authority of the prescribing physician, veterinary surgeon, or dentist, uses any prescription to sell any drug on more than one occasion, shall be guilty of a criminal offence and shall be liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars and costs and not less than five hundred dollars and costs, or to imprisonment for a t^rm not exceeding one year, or to both fine and imprisonment."
The other change I propose is to ask the committee to substitute for subsection (4) of the Bill as it was printed the following clause:
The provisions of section five-
Is that the new Bill?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I purpose to substitute a new section for subsection (4) of section 5A as follows:
" (4) (a) The provisions of section five and of paragraphs (e) and (f) of this section shall not apply to the possession, sale, or distribution by a druggist carrying on a business in a bona fide drug store of preparations and remedies which do not contain more than two grains of opium or more than one-fourth of a grain of morphine, or more than one-eighth of a grain of heroin, or more than one grain of codeine, or any salt or derivative of any of them in one fluid ounce, or, if a solid or semi-solid preparation, in one avoirdupois ouncfe; or to liniments, ointments, or other preparations which are prepared for external skin use only, which do not contain cocaine or any of its salts or preparations, but every such remedy or preparation as mentioned in this section, must contain active medicinal drugs other than narcotic in sufficient proportion to confer upon the preparation or remedy valuable medicinal qualities, other than those possessd by the narcotic drugs alone;

provided, however, that it shall be an offence against this Act to sell, or offer for sale, any remedy or preparation intended for internal use, which contains opium, morphine, heroin or codeine, unless there be printed in a conspicuous place on .an inseparable part of the main panel of the label and wrapper of the bottle, box, or other container, and in letters of the same size and visability as the word that dominates the label, in (the article) the following words:-
It is unlawful to administer this preparation to a child under two years of age as it contains (insert name of drug) and Is dangerous to its life.
Provided, further, that the Governor in Council may, by regulation to be published in the Canada Gazette, extend and apply the provisions of the said paragraphs (e) and (f) to any preparation named or described in such regulation.
(b)	It shall be an offence against this Act for any person to sell for administration to a child under two years of age, or to administer to any such child any remedy or preparation containing opium, morphine, heroin or codeine the sale of which is permitted by this subsection.
(c)	Nothing in this Act shall contravene or affect any provisions of the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act or any amendments thereto.
Just a word in explanation of that amendment. The International Opium Convention does not apply to the sale of preparations containing a limited quantity of these drugs. The quantities mentioned in this subsection are smaller than those mentioned in the Treaty, but are the same as those mentioned in the Harrison Act-the American Act passed some two or three years ago to deal with this same subject matter.
I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to: debate adjourned.
On motion of Rt. Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
Monday, April 26, 1920.
